HENRICUS DACUS
(HENRIK HARPESTRENG)

ON SIMPLE LAXATIVE MEDICINES

PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME

BY

J.W. S. JOHNSSON

COPENHAGEN
VILHELM PRIOR'S ROYAL COURT BOOKSHOP

1914

TO

MY FRIEND AND TEACHER

Dr. PAUL DORVEAUX
LIBRARIAN AT THE ÉCOLE SUPÉRIEURE DE PHARMACIE, PARIS

While searching through the Royal Library's medical manuscripts, undertaken with the aim of, if possible, expanding knowledge of Danish physicians in the Middle Ages, I came across in Manuscript G. k. S. 1654, 4° a treatise, De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, written by a hitherto unknown author, Henricus Dacus or de Dacia. The manuscript in question is well known, not least on account of its containing a Macer text, but the treatise by Henricus Dacus appears until now not to have been noticed, not even by C. Molbech, who nevertheless discusses the manuscript in detail in a note on page 39 of Henrik Harpestreng's Danish Medical Book, Copenhagen 1826.

Having read the treatise, I conducted some investigations into the identity of Henricus de Dacia, and I formed the impression that the said author and Henrik Harpestreng were the same person, without however being able to produce conclusive proof. Due to a journey abroad, the work had to be set aside for the time being, and during my absence I sent my interpretation of the manuscript's text to Dr. phil. Marius Kristensen, Askov, partly to obtain help with the more difficult passages, and partly so that he, as editor of the Nordic Harpestreng texts, could express his opinion on the treatise and its author. It was indeed also Dr. Kristensen who established the identity between Henricus de Dacia and Henrik Harpestreng.

It will always present difficulties to produce an edition of a manuscript known only in a single copy, especially when that copy frequently contains misunderstandings and was not made with great precision. In the present case I have chosen, precisely on account of the copy's incompleteness, to let the text speak for itself

myself, and thus only exceptionally to correct errors and misunderstandings, just as I have not attempted to fill in missing words and sentences. This applies particularly to the Introduction, which in its present linguistic form is quite incomprehensible. The places in the text that seem to me entirely corrupted are marked with † placed before the relevant sentence, and punctuation has been added to ease comprehension. As for the frequently used sign ℥, I have read this as uncia. The sign is not found recorded in the commonly used palaeographic handbooks, and I have found justification for my reading in the fact that ½ pound was equal to 8 ounces, which is why one also finds in the section on fumus terræ: libra semis vel VIII ℥. I must however note that Avicenna (see the note sextum, p. 93) uses cotylus, where Henricus de Dacia has ℥, even though the texts otherwise agree. This need not involve any contradiction, since cotylus was most often equal to a libra, but its value was variable.
During the preparation of this work I have received help from many quarters. First and foremost I owe thanks to Dr. phil. Marius Kristensen for his repeatedly ready assistance. I also owe thanks to Professors J. L. Heiberg and Verner Dahlerup for advice and guidance, and particularly for the recommendations that gave me access to having this work published here in the country. A similar heartfelt thanks must also go to the Board of the Carlsberg Foundation, which granted the funds necessary for publication, and to Dr. V. Kuhr, who has been my tireless helper with linguistic difficulties.
A number of foreign scholars have conducted research on my behalf in libraries and archives in their home regions or have given me valuable assistance in other ways. I am thus indebted to Dr. Paul Dorveaux, librarian at the École supérieure de Pharmacie in Paris, Dr. Ernest Wickersheimer, librarian at the Académie de Médecine in Paris, and to Dr. Paul Delaunay in Le Mans. Furthermore, Dr. Garsonnier, archivist Jacques Soyer, and librarian A. Cagnieu have examined archives and libraries in Orléans on my behalf. Among German scholars, Hofrat, Dr. med. (h. c.) Max Höfler, of Bad Tölz near Munich, has repeatedly been of assistance to me. I ask them all to accept my warmest and most heartfelt thanks.

By dedicating my work to Dr. Paul Dorveaux, I have attempted to repay a small part of my debt to him. He was the first to forge the connection between France and the Danish physicians who occupy themselves with the history of medicine. Many Danes have over the years sought his help, but none have sought it in vain — least of all myself. The present work should therefore also serve as a token of the warm devotion I feel for my long-standing teacher and friend.

J. W. S. JOHNSSON.

February 1914.

The treatise that is here to be published for the first time bears the title: De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, and its author is a hitherto unknown Henricus de Dacia, also referred to as Henricus Dacus. The treatise is included in a miscellany, G. k. S. 1654, 4°, in the Royal Library in Copenhagen, a volume that also contains writings of Johannes Parisiensis, Mattheus Platearius, Nicolaus and Macer, along with some smaller pieces, among which one bears the title Anbaleon. Henricus de Dacia's text occupies folios 104r–110r.

A question immediately arises: who is this author? Is it a hitherto unknown medieval author from Denmark, or should Dacia here be understood as belonging to one of the three Nordic kingdoms? The name Dacia, of course, commonly means Denmark, but it is also used to denote the mendicant orders' provincial division. For the investigation it would be significant to determine within what period Henricus de Dacia lived, since the Dominican Order came to Denmark in the year 1221 and the Franciscans the following year, and Dacia would thus be confirmed as Denmark if Henricus de Dacia's life and work fell before those years.

No author of the mentioned name appears to be known to Nordic bibliographers. H. Schück¹ mentions no Henricus Dacus, and Ellen Jørgensen² does not either. The manuscript itself gives no information—

¹ H. Schück: Nordiska Medeltidsförfattere, an article included in Bibliografiska och litteratur-historiska Anteckningar, Uppsala 1896, p. 120.
² Ellen Jørgensen: Om nogle middelalderlige Forfattere, der nævnes som hjemmehørende i "Dacia". Historisk Tidsskrift, 8 R III, 1911, p. 234.
Fr. Grøn, in a lecture at the Kristiania Academy of Sciences on 24 April 1908 (published in Norsk Magazin for Lægevidenskab 1908, No. 10, under the title: Nogle

concerning who the author of the little Treatise is. It was written down around 1400–1450, collected in Erfurt (f 184v: hec collecta sunt Erfordie) and donated as a gift to the Convent of Maria in Segeberg (f 1r: liber domus sanctissime virginis marie et sancti Johannis ewangeliste in segeberghe per dominum luderum breme donatus).

A Henricus de Dacia is, however, not entirely unknown, since in M. s. fr. 1357, 2° (15th century) in the Bibliothèque impériale (now the National Library) in Paris, a certain Henry de Danemarche is mentioned. The note about him is included in Symon de Pharès: Receuil des plus célèbres astrologues et de quelques hommes doctes. The relevant passage¹ reads:

[f 119r] Master Henry de Danemarche, excellent physician in Orleans and great astrologer of his time, made many singular predictions, judgments, and prognostications, and among other things predicted the exile of the Jews from France. One of the causes was that in the said Orleans it came to pass that a priest was singing mass, and after he had consecrated the body of J. C., when he wished to take it, it suddenly appeared all bloody, which King Philip² heard of, and he and the people of the city rushed there and saw the sacrament in the form of a piece of flesh like Inde[?], and upon the corporals there appeared drops of blood. A similar miracle appeared at Vritour[?] in Vendôme and another in the city of Arras in a castle called Sezamis, and these occurred around the time that King Philip² had the city of Paris paved and the Bois de Vincennes enclosed, in the year 1181.

Remarks on Medieval Medical Knowledge in the North mentioned newer parchment finds in Norway containing fragments of medieval authors' medical writings. He mentions Henrik Harpestreng, but no Henricus de Dacia. It would moreover have been somewhat outside the scope of the lecture to discuss personalities in greater detail, as it is primarily concerned with the influence of medieval schools on Norwegian medical practice.
¹ Count P. Riant: Et Bidrag til Vestigia Danorum extra Daniam in Chr. Bruun and O. Nielsen, Danske Samlinger 1866–67, p. 270. Since Count Riant had omitted a passage in his copy of the manuscript (from en maniere to Sezamis), I obtained a copy of the entire relevant section through the librarian of the Académie de Médecine in Paris, Dr. Er. Wickersheimer. I warmly thank him here for his tireless helpfulness, so often called upon by Danes.
² Philippe II or Philippe Auguste (1165–1223). Even the briefest biographies mention his work in beautifying Paris. He built the Castle of Vincennes.

12

There is no doubt here that we are dealing with a Danish man, and that Henricus de Dacia was also Danish and not Nordic, may well be established by the fact that in the Explicit of the Treatise he is referred to as Henricus Dacus. As for the identity of the two figures, it is impossible to say anything definitive, even though it might be reasonable to assume that both merged into a single third person, the well-known Henrik Harpestreng, familiar from his herbals, lapidaries, and medical books, whose year of death is given as 1244, a year that is, however, hardly entirely certain¹. The situation now is, however, that Henrik Harpestreng's life and career are so extraordinarily little known — one knows essentially only that he was Medicus et Canonicus Roschildensis, and that he was King Erik's (Plovpennings?) physician — that it is at present impossible to find points of connection with what has already been presented. We shall now see whether a comparison between the Harpestreng writings and Henricus de Dacia's Treatise can contribute to an understanding of both it and its author's identity. How the relationship to Henry de Danemarche stands will be discussed later.

¹ The year 1244 is given by many authors (Arild Huitfeld, J. Langebek, P. F. Suhm). It is also found in Erik Pontoppidan, who cites an epitaph that Harpestreng himself is said to have written.

HENRICUS DACUS
ON SIMPLE LAXATIVE MEDICINES

Avicenna says in the book on simples that all medicines of simple laxative virtue have a certain preparatory purpose, and among physicians it is established that some are particularly suited to this use. The laxative simples, by their inherent quality, depend on repositories and, as stated by Italian and other authors, do not work without diligent attention to requirements; they produce a movement which purges certain medicines, and their laxative virtues, described in order, and set down as to which collection from the plants, and which compound medicines, and which collections of simples and their capacities are as follows:

Aloe — Of rhubarb — Of myrobalans
Agaric — Of dragagant — Of [various roots]
Armenian [clay] — Of quince — Of myrobalans [second variety]
[Various simples] — Of white ebulus — Of polypody
[Various simples] — Of black ebulus — Of rhubarb
Absinth — Of euphorbium — Of [herb]
Hellebore — Of hepatic [herb] — Of fumitory
Bdellium — Of gula — Of nettle
Centaury — Of fumitory — Of senna

Cucumber [wild] — Of fibula

Milk and the juice in a potion: it draws down and moves the stomach; it purifies and drives away vapors rising to the head, and drives them downward. For new uses, and for the treatment of idle animals and their conditions, suitable for hemorrhoidal remedy. Whoever needs the preparatory part should take it before: dragagant, or bdellium, or a little mastic, or milk. Before taking items of hepatic kind, it is praiseworthy and effective in loosening others, and when two [remedies] are joined, the administration is such that after five days the odors begin to diminish, and old colors and old virtues are restored; for virtue is best when it is drawn off with water or brine, and the strength is confirmed.

Simples

Take of these things half a dram, 4 parts in the compound, a medicine for the mouth; and 2 parts of small scruples; for simple drinking the lesser dose is 1 dram, the greater 2 drams, and alone it is slow to act, best taken before sleep for eating it brings benefit.

   In fevers it opens the bowels on both sides, and for the grosser humors it releases bile, clearing obstructions of the joints, helping those afflicted by numbness and mortification; if one is fasting on legumes and bathing, and better with white foods, the simple dose of these things is 1 dram, the lesser half, for another medicine of these things there is a purging effect.

   It is noted that against jaundice and melancholy this plant is sovereign against dropsy, pleurisy, certain fevers, palsy and arthritis. The dose of these things, middle measure: take 1 dram and a half dissolved in water of liquorice; the greater dose is 3, the lesser 2.

   One scruple, as the diet says, should take away yellowness and melancholy; the patient should attend carefully, not taking it too minutely, 4 times, to be ministered to for recovery. The middle dose is 3 drams, the greater 3 and a half, the lesser 2 and a half.

   For water gathered in the belly, purging the colon, take 2 drams more than sufficient; for the preparation of the decoction the dried root is best placed in boiling water so that the patient drinks it once a day at the fourth hour; not to exceed the middle dose; the drink should be taken through a tube of dried water, about one pound; it drives out the colon, makes the body thin from swelling, and cleanses of leprosy.

   Of asafoetida multiply as needed. For those constipated: for small bile passages, for hardness of the colon and for the gravel of the liver, and against mucus in the lungs, and for colic, it does not allow torpor to settle; its odor is of musk, and 4 parts suffice; against the evil vapors it absorbs bitterness, for four virtues it opens the opportunity for good function; it lasts, purifying the vessels and cleansing the belly, collecting mucus and binding it; against sweating take the juice; the dose is 2 drams, and its juice is the dose; the correction of the dose is 6 parts greater, the lesser 2; if one desires the best benefit:

   Of myrobolans: take dried myrobolans, and also of dried rose-hips, and also of gall-apples and aloe and acacia, which strengthens and dignifies the head; and also of the flower of [illegible] make a decoction for use.

GALEN says in his book on simple medicine that every simple laxative medicine has an attracting power upon its proper humors. It is therefore necessary for a physician to know what each simple laxative medicine properly purges; for from knowledge of these depends knowledge of compound medicines. And because among physicians there is error in this matter — those who have the books of Galen and other ancient authors but either do not possess them or have not studied them with diligence — at the request of my companions I have undertaken to write down the virtues and doses of certain medicines, more generally of laxatives, and afterward to append certain rules concerning the administration of medicines, concerning electuaries, concerning collections of simple medicines, and their preservation.

ALOE is hot and dry in the second degree; by secondary action it draws out red bile and thick humors from the stomach, purges the brain of the same choleric and phlegmatic gross humors, and prevents vapors from rising from the stomach to the head, and therefore purges humors in the optic nerve and between the coats of the eye where they have gathered, and opens the mouths of hemorrhoids. Whoever therefore suffers from hemorrhoids needs to take it; let him take it with tragacanth or with a little bdellium or mastic. There are three species of aloe. By hepatic aloe we understand the following: it is more praiseworthy and more useful for loosening than the other two; it has a radiance like that of yellow gum, a more pleasant odor than the other species, breaks easily, is of a color resembling liver; old aloe is of little virtue, but fresh aloe is of more perfect virtue, whose use is most opportune if it is washed in water or simple goat's whey. Its medium dose is one drachma, and in compound medicines 3 scruples and 2 quarter-scruples; when taken by itself, the lesser dose is 5 I, the greater dose 5 III; its action is slow, and therefore one should not rush to eat after taking it.

AGARIC is hot and dry, hot in the second degree, dry in the third; it loosens both bile and thick phlegm, is moderate in its action, draws from the remote parts of the body...

19

of the body's poison, it remedies the harms of deadly potions and drinks. If taken in electuaries, the white Agaricus with its brightness is better; it is easy to break. The medium dose of this simple drink is 5 I, the greater dose is one exagium, the lesser is 5 semis; when taken with another medicine the dose is one exagium semis.

ARMONIACUM is warm and dry in the third degree. Its particular virtue is to purge phlegm and melancholy; it benefits those suffering from dropsy, diseases of the spleen, migraine, paralysis, and arthritis. Its medium dose is 5 I and a half, taken in plain water or milk-water; the greater dose is 5 III, the lesser 5 II.

ACUANUM, that is scorulo as Dioscorides calls it, purges phlegm and melancholy. It should be rubbed in water and ground carefully but not too finely, and mixed with oxymel. The medium dose is 5 III, the greater dose is 5 III and a half, the lesser 5 II and a half.

WHEY purges red and black bile. The simple drink is worth more; the dose is one libra, and if spikenard is cooked in it, it removes yellow water. Its dose is two parts of one libra, to be drunk once a day. For one who cannot drink it, let him take over many days half a libra of whey; it gently draws out burnt and red bile, and frees the body from dry ulcers, leprosy, and similar conditions.

ABSINTHIUM (wormwood) is hot and dry, yet it comes in many varieties; the best and most praiseworthy is of saffron color, having a soft down like the feathers of newly hatched pigeons, with a pleasant smell like that of hepatic aloe, and it has nodes in it. Its taste is strongly bitter with a certain astringency. It has the particular virtue of opening obstructions; it cures jaundice, cleanses the blood in the veins, purges red and black bile, cleanses the stomach of all unnatural bile; it draws together a loosened stomach, and powerfully purges black bile when compounded with epithyme, if its juice is taken. The dose is 3 drams; if a decoction of it is taken, the dose is 6 drams; the greater dose is four scruples, either somewhat less or somewhat more.

BELLIRICI have a cold and dry virtue; their actions are similar to those of citrine myrobalans. But they are of weaker action, and when used together with oak galls, henna, and vinegar, they strongly blacken the hair.

BDELLIUM is hot and moist; it has the virtue of loosening phlegm when drunk; the simple dose is 2 drams; when given with honey-water, half an exagium given with Indian, belleric, or kabuli myrobalans is beneficial for hemorrhoids and joint ailments located in the anus. Bdellium when hot and dry has the virtue of loosening phlegm.

CENTAUREA (centaury) is hot and dry; the finer variety is better; it purges red bile and viscous mixed phlegm, and is beneficial for joint pain, sciatica, and colic. Its juice is not drunk but used by physicians as a decoction. Its dose is

The decoction taken as a drink is 2 exagia; in enemas however 5 scruples V. But its juice can be cooked and strained and given to drink, and the dose is 1 scruple and a half, and the dose as an enema is 4 scruples.

THE PITH OF THE GARDEN CROCUS is hot and dry, purges phlegm, treats dropsy, which I have proven, and benefits those suffering from colic. Its dose is 5 scruples V with a little oregano or Indian salt.

CASSIA FISTULA is hot and moist, purges by lubricating and drawing out, loosens gently, purges bile, expels hardened matter together with a little turbith, and relieves the pain of colic in the patient; yet without any other medicine it draws out gross humors, just as turbith does, and we say that turbith given together with cassia fistula draws out phlegmatic humors which, given alone, it is not sufficient to expel. Cassia fistula given with tamarinds expels bile; given with the juice of nightshade or the juice of fresh coriander it is beneficial in tertian fevers, and used as a gargle it dissolves an abscess of the throat. Cassia fistula is better when it is in the pod, and better still when the pod is thick and strong, which is the opposite of almonds.

WILD CUCUMBERS are hot and dry in substance, similar to citron plums, and they have both bitterness and sharpness. The bitterness is lesser, the sharpness greater; they loosen thick and viscous phlegm, also black bile, and citrine bile, the water of dropsical patients; they benefit those suffering from phlegmatic conditions and from migraine, paralytics and those with colic. But it should be noted that it is not safe to take them plain, since

22

They are very strong. They should therefore be mixed with cassia fistula or with Aloe. Of these, however, they are better when collected at the setting of the Pleiades. If it is asked why we say that this [!] is the time of their completion — because those of them that are citrine in color are better, their juice is better in taste and substance, and the juice should not be expressed except by the strength of the hands or feet, and therefore take care not to grind them themselves. But if you wish to preserve it, pour off the clear water; keep the juice that appears after the residue until it thickens, so that you can make troches; make them and keep them for two parts of the year in their full strength, and after that their virtue diminishes. The dose taken by mouth is one half-scruple. If you wish to moderate its strength, add a little gum of the elders, or gum arabic, and a little wheat starch.

COLOQUINTIDA is hot and dry in the second degree; its pulp purges phlegm from the brain and the optic nerve and from the stomach, and prevents phlegmatic vapors from rising, and draws phlegm from the deep parts of the body. It is most praiseworthy when collected of saffron color at the setting of the Pleiades, for then it is perfect and complete. When incomplete it causes vomiting, dejection, sadness, disturbance, anxiety, and failure of breath, if it is given carelessly. And at times the medicine should be used with caution in great heat; moreover, the fat of the coloquintida outside its rind loses its strength within three months. It should therefore be kept safe, and since the flesh is rarely collected, we no longer recommend it; rather, let its harshness be tempered with a little gum arabic. Its average dose is two and a half scruples with gum arabic, and one and a half scruples without gum.

DIAGRIDIUM, that is scammony, is hot and dry in the third degree; it is most praiseworthy when fresh, tending toward a clear warmth, white with a clean, fine, glaucous surface, easily broken; such is found in Antioch. It purges red bile and its varieties, such as the citrine, green, leek-green, and rust-colored, as well as the phlegmatic humors with which it is mixed in the body. It purges with strong virtue, but because it tends to cause disturbance, cramping, and excoriation of the intestines, it must not be used except with caution. Its violence is broken by cooking it in the capsules of quince seeds. It is likewise corrected with Aloe and myrobalans and the juice of quinces and their decoction water, and when quince is placed in preparations with scammony itself, it is of faster action and less harmful. From quinces let a kind of electuary be made and the scammony placed in it. The simple dose is one-third of a dram, together with things that temper its virtue, or when it is cooked the dose is half a scruple and ten grains; the larger dose is one scruple.

EPITHYMUM is hot and dry at the beginning of the third degree. Its property is to purge black bile; for those who have an excess of red bile it is not suitable, indeed it is harmful, for it is proven that it causes them disturbance and upheaval. It is useful for those suffering from red bile, burnt black bile, and natural black bile. It is beneficial for the elderly and the aged, for it cleanses their bodies of melancholy. Epithymum is most praiseworthy when its color tends toward red and it has a strong odor. The simple drinking dose is 2 drams and a half, the lesser dose 2 drams, the greater 3 drams; the decoction dose is 7 drams, the lesser 5 drams, the greater 9 drams. And when you wish to use simple epithymum, boil water and remove it from the fire until it cools somewhat, then add the ground epithymum and stir.

24

Mix well and offer the mixture to be drunk. But if you wish to give a decoction together with other herbs, first cook the other herbs thoroughly and strain them, then add epithymum and leave it there until the strained liquid cools, and give it to drink. If you wish to give epithymum in its own substance together with a laxative decoction, cook the laxatives and afterwards strain the strained liquid, allow it to cool somewhat, then add 2 drams or 1 dram and a half of epithymum, mix it, and give it to drink. And it should be known that epithymum does not need any correction from another medicine; on the contrary, it corrects other medicines itself.


ELLEBORUS ALBUS is hot and dry in the third degree. The more praiseworthy kind is whiter and more uniform in texture. Its property is to purge thick phlegm, and more by vomiting than from below, as we shall describe in what follows.


ELLEBORUS NIGER is hot and dry in the third degree. Its particular property is to purge red and black bile. The most praiseworthy kind is fresh and genuinely black, of a quality midway between fine and coarse in substance; it is beneficial for madness arising from melancholy. It removes dark skin blemishes when used as an ointment; it is beneficial in leprosy and elephantiasis and in all diseases arising from black bile. The simple dose to be drunk is 2 obols, the larger dose half a scruple. It should, however, be given together with a decoction of epithymum, and its potency is corrected by that; and if we do not have epithymum, let it be given with a decoction of savory, one third of a scruple, and it is proven that it is better given with a decoction of both of these together in equal parts.

EUPHORBIUM is hot and dry in the fourth degree, of sharp strength. It is better when new, bright and lemon-yellow, and of strong odor. Its property is to purge watery matter from those with white phlegm, and phlegm from the joints and veins. It is beneficial for migraines, paralytics, and those with sciatica; it is not given by itself, but is therefore administered together with other medicines. The dose is a middle one of nine grains, the lesser six, the greater truly fourteen; it should be ground but not too finely, and in this form it should not be drunk, because it causes sadness, agitation, upset of the mouth and stomach, compression, sweating and weakness. So that these side effects may be avoided, the prescribed quantity is observed and there is added to it a little gum arabic of a weight of four or three grains. All those of a warm constitution and those in whom bile and blood predominate should beware of Euphorbium.

EUPATORIUM is hot and dry; it purges black bile. Hence it treats quartan fevers and apostemes, melancholy of the intestines, quintan fevers, and chronic fevers much aggravated by phlegm, when used with a decoction of agrimony. The dose at that time is two scruples and a half; if its juice is drunk, a half exagium with oxymel, it cures a true and established quartan fever. But if its decoction is given by itself, it is effective against the aforementioned, though in that case its dose is two drams, the lesser three, the greater six.

ESULA is hot in the third degree, dry in the second; it has both sharpness and a biting quality. Better is that whose color tends toward red. It is light in weight. In substance [106 v] it is fine; when prepared together with leather it is of dark color, of coarse substance, difficult to break, thorny; it is most harmful because it causes agitation, twisting, and oppression in the mouth and sto-

machi. Esula praiseworthy dissolves yellow water, phlegm, and the thick moisture of the joints; it helps with colic arising from phlegm and greasiness, and also loosens black bile. It has a milky juice, but its milk has no usefulness for loosening. Whoever wishes to suppress the harmful quality of esula should steep it for a day and night in sweet milk, and change the milk three or four times per day and night — I say day and night because if it is left longer it loses its virtue, or becomes too weakened. Afterward it should be removed from the milk, dried in the shade, and then powdered. If you wish to give it on its own, give it with anise and fennel or with a decoction of them. If it is given against colic from flatulence or thick phlegm, add roasted cumin and oxymel. If you wish to cure dropsical leucophlegmatic patients or those with general swelling (anasarca), after the herb has been steeped in milk, dried, and powdered, infuse it in water of nightshade and of fennel-flower, in equal parts, for three days; then strain the liquid and dry it in the shade until you can make lozenges. But first add a little Indian salt, or turbit, or both, or myrobalan, or aloe with turbit or Indian salt; and if you add a small amount of all of them it causes no harm, and it drives out yellow water gently and with good and great effect. Make the lozenges of this weight: one scruple, and let it be given with water of fennel and oxymel. In the other aforesaid diseases the dose is two drams, the lesser dose is half a scruple, and the greater is two and a half drams.

FUMITORY is cold and dry in nature. It has a certain bitterness that carries heat away from the stomach, it loosens red bile and purges it from burnt superfluities; gently but effectively it helps with itching and scabies arising from poisonous and burnt humors in the flesh and skin, and with leprosy. Upon reading through it, the present treatise reveals itself as belonging to the works that originally emanated from the Salernitan School. It is therefore no accident that it has been included in a volume containing almost exclusively writings by authors originating from that place. A comparison with the Harpestreng writings reveals two major differences. First and foremost, the present work is written in Latin, in contrast to all the Harpestreng writings, which are known only in versions in the Nordic languages; secondly, the treatise is a scholarly work that, by its very form, addresses a learned audience, indeed perhaps a body of listeners, as certain expressions suggest. The Harpestreng writings, by contrast, address the common people, and the language alone demonstrates this, while the degree to which they have become the property of laymen hardly needs to be mentioned here. If Henricus Dacus is the same person as Henrik Harpestreng, we would then be standing for the first time before a scholarly work by the most celebrated Danish physician of the Middle Ages. And that the two persons are identical is proven by the fact that the treatise on laxative remedies contains the original text for the 81st section of the Herb Book — a passage for which no author, or rather no source, had previously been known, and which in the Danish textual version is in part translated word for word from the Latin, but which, it must be admitted, has at the same time been so substantially altered and abbreviated that comprehension, which in certain places is quite difficult, has suffered as a result. As a whole, the chapter also gives a somewhat scattered and patchwork impression. A comparison of the relevant passages will show how closely the two texts follow one another. I reprint here the Danish text and also the relevant passages from Henricus Dacus' treatise, since the section in its entirety has been published in the collected text (pp. 31–34).

That Rhazes (850–923 (932)) is explicitly named in the text is perhaps due to the fact that he marks the introduction and beginning of "the Arabic art of medicine." He genuinely renewed medical study in several ways, not least by attempting to bring chemistry into the service of medical science.

After this, it seems as though "De simplicibus medicinis laxativis" belongs to a somewhat later period than the Herb Books. Yet this is by no means certain. It is hardly likely that Harpestreng, when writing the Herb Books, would have included drugs that the common man in every case would have found difficult to obtain, and which had perhaps only recently gained wider recognition in learned medical science. It is more reasonable to suppose that he deliberately omitted such things and only mentioned them in treatises addressed to a different stratum of the population than the layman. It is also quite characteristic that the texts converge precisely at the point where the concern was to give rules for the sick — rules that could be used by all and sundry.

Modestino del Gaizo, who according to De Renzi, Daremberg, and Henschel has taken the Salerno school as his subject of investigation¹, states that it passed through five different periods in its development. The first he calls the cenobitical, and it falls before the year 1000. The next period extends a hundred and fifty years further in time, during which ancient medicine experienced its rebirth. The third, the 12th century, is characterized by the popular and hygienic nature of the medical art, while the surgical schools were established in the fourth period, the 13th century. The period of decline lasted from the fourteenth century until 1811.

It remains to investigate whether "Maistre Henry de Danemarche" could be identical with Henrik Harpestreng. It cannot be proven, but there is some likelihood of it, or at least it is not impossible. From very ancient times there has been a lively connection between France and Denmark. La Porte du Theil¹, who devoted particular attention to relations between the two countries in the 12th century, and who gives extensive account of their rich political and scholarly intercourse, even asserts that the connection with France was, for Denmark's part, more lively than with any other country. For the 13th–15th centuries, Er. Wickersheimer has provided some information², showing what esteem Danish physicians enjoyed in France. However, no Henricus Dacus is mentioned by these authors, nor is he found mentioned in Budinszky's³ list of Danes who studied at the University of Paris during the Middle Ages⁴. The account of "Maistre Henry de Danemarche" is localized to Orléans, which is yet further evidence of the great role that city played for Danish scholars. Elsewhere I have given an account—

It was founded around 1150, and the first document relating to it is dated January 1180³, a point in time when Henry de Danemarche was presumably already in Orléans.

45

Simon de Pharès's note establishes with certainty that the year 1181 was the time of the miracle that occurred, which must coincide with the period of Henry de Danemarche's stay in Orléans. If this Henry is indeed identical with Henrik Harpestreng, then the latter must have died as a very old man. Between the two years, 73 years have passed, and since the Danish scholars set out on their travels abroad while still quite young, Henrik Harpestreng must have reached an age of around ninety years, which admittedly could lie within the bounds of possibility. It can therefore certainly not be established that the two persons are identical.

When one considers the relationship between Harpestreng's Herbal and the present article, De simplicibus medicinis laxativis, the question arises whether Harpestreng first wrote his books in Latin and later partly used them for what one might call more popular writings. Whether this is the case, or whether his work as an author falls into two parts — a scholarly one, which unfortunately is still very little known, and a popular one, which long ago earned him a reputation throughout all of Scandinavia — is not known. These questions cannot be answered at present. The manuscript discussed here is the only one that has so far come to light under the name of Henrik Dacus, and despite much searching I have not succeeded in finding more. Such will surely come to light, however, as the great libraries' manuscript collections are registered and worked through.

In one respect the present manuscript is remarkable, namely in that it originates from Germany, from Erfurt. It would therefore be of interest to try to learn something about how it came to Denmark, but here again the search proves elusive, and one is left with possibilities. A connection between Denmark and Erfurt can be demonstrated in the period 1400–1450, which roughly corresponds to the manuscript's time of writing, in that Knud Mikkelsen, who was matriculated at Rostock in 1421, later went to Erfurt and took his Master's degree there in 1425. He became Rector of the University there in the winter of 1434–35 and Doctor juris utriusque. In 1451 he was appointed Bishop of Viborg. However, nothing is known about the books,

46

he presumably brought with him to Denmark, and nothing is known to indicate that this learned man occupied himself with the art of medicine. That his name has been connected with the so-called "Regimen contra pestilentiam domini Kanuti Episcopi Arusiensis" is certainly due to attempts to establish who this Bishop Knud was, and not to Knud Mikkelsen's work in the field of medicine. It cannot, however, be denied that there is a possibility that Knud Mikkelsen may have had the Harpestreng Treatise copied in Erfurt with the purpose of making a famous compatriot's work known in a place where his own scholarly work had found such great appreciation. But all of this is conjecture; regarding the manuscript's origin, nothing whatsoever is known beyond what it itself reveals.

The first section of Henricus Dacus' text has been commented upon principally following Ibn al-Baytar's pharmacognosy in Leclerce's translation. In the commentary, which opens with some brief remarks of a historical and botanical nature, only what directly bore upon the text has been included, and I have regarded it as lying outside my task to give a more extensive description of the position of the drugs within the systems of classification or of their methods of application. Some of the cited Arabic authors are known only through Ibn al-Baytar; as a rule I have used Leclerce's spelling for their names.
The commentary to the following sections has, however, been worked out on the basis of Avicenna, supplemented from other authors. Since the source text was unknown, it has been important to me, through extensive quotations from the authors mentioned, to show what changes, and how great, had been made to the original text by Henricus Dacus' treatment of it.

GALENUS SAYS: see De simpl. medic. temp. ac. facult., book III (Kühn XI p. 589 and 759), as well as the second chapter in De purgant. medicament. facult. (Kühn XI p. 327). This latter work has in some Galen editions (e.g. Venetiis, apud Juntas MDLXV) the heading: That each medicine has the power to attract its own proper humor, as proven by experience.

ALOE is the thick-flowing, bitter juice of various aloe species. It has not been definitively established from which plants the ancient drug was derived (see Berendes' commentary on Dioscorides). Galen mentions that it was obtained from Syria magna, Coele-Syria and Arabia, but that the best came from India, and it was that variety which was introduced under the name Aloe. Dioscorides gives India and Arabia as its place of origin, but also lands by the sea and certain islands, e.g. Andros. Constantinus Africanus (p. 354) mentions Socotra and Persia.
Aloe is mentioned in Harpestraeng's herbal books (S. 60; K. U¹ XIIII; C. 89).
calidum: The text follows Constantinus: Universally, aloe is hot and dry in the 2nd degree. Mesue, however, says: hot in the second degree, dry in the third, but Avicenna (II. 2. p. 105v) establishes: It is hot in the second, dry in the same and is said to be hot and dry in the third: but this is not so.
humores grossos a stomacho: According to Galen, aloe was a remedy that cleansed the intestines well, but not the whole body. If one wished to achieve specific effects, one therefore had to give it together with other medicines. He counted aloe among the mildly purging remedies.
purgat cerebrum ...... et prohibet vapores ascendere: The Arabs understood the action of aloe as follows: after the medicine had been absorbed in the intestines, the light and fine vapors thereby released rose

50

Vapors rising to the Head and Brain were cleansed of harmful fluids that had accumulated there, originating from pituita and from vapors that rose up from the Ventricle toward the Head. For this to happen, the Aloe vapors had to penetrate all Tissue, including the Optic Nerve, which was conceived of as hollow like a quill case. The harmful humores were thereby driven out and Vision was improved. (Hobeïch ibn el-Hassan, cited after Ibn el Beïthar).

vapores: El Farecy (after Ibn el Beïthar) states that Aloe warms the Stomach, strengthens it, and dispels intestinal gas.

humores in nervo visus: see the note purgat cerebrum. Its effect on the Eyes is discussed by many Authors (Dioscorides, Avicenna, Rhazes and several other Arabic writers). Some state that Aloe helps against Cataract. (Oribas. II. 267, Honein and others).

emorroidis: est maxime nocens emorroidibus et ano (Mesuë: de simplicibus f. XXXIIv, Sp. 2). Mahraris (in Ibn el Beïthar) holds that Aloe helps neither the Liver nor Hemorrhoids.

dragagant: Tragacanth was used for cold Constitutions, Bdellium for warm ones. If there was a Ventricular or Liver condition present, Mastix was given (Mansoury in Ibn el Beïthar). Mesuë (l. c.) says much the same as H. Dacus: rectificando ipsum cum administratione bdellii cum eo: aut dragaganti aut masticis et similium. Mesuë writes somewhat later that Bdellium and Tragacanth are the best Rectifiers, and Constantinus Afric. states that Aloe taken frequently and in large Doses injures the Stomach and Intestines, which is why it is given in Preparations combined with the three aforementioned Things.

Aloe tres sunt species: Galen (de simpl. medic. facult. lib. VI c. 23) writes: "This herb does not grow very abundantly among us, and that which grows in greater Syria is more watery and of weaker potency. But in warmer regions, such as Coelosyria and Arabia, it is much better. The best is the Indian variety, whose juice is that which is imported to us under the name Aloe." In the Middle Ages three kinds of Aloe were distinguished: 1. Aloe socotrina, which came from Socotora and was considered the best. It was also called lucida. 2. Aloe hepatica, whose liver-like color indicated that it was less pure. The third kind, Aloe caballina, was used only in Veterinary medicine and consisted of the residues left behind in the preparation vessels. Aloe he-

51

patica was also called arabica, while the Arabic names asman-
djang and sunhang were used for the third variety (Hobeïch ibn el Has-
san). Mesuë has four varieties: succutrina, persica, armenica and ara-
bica. Constantinus Afric. has red Aloe from India, black from Persia
and yellow from Arabia.

gumini: The Arabic physicians did not compare Aloe with
gummi croceæ, but with gummi arabicum. Aloe socotrina was
saffron-yellow, easy to break, and the fractured surfaces shone like Arabic
Gum. Aloe arabica was darker, lighter in weight, and the fracture
shone only a little. Asmandjäng's fracture did not shine, and it was
not yellow, but rather blackish.

odoris iocundi: When one breathed upon Aloe hepatica, one would
obtain a scent like that of Myrrh (Abu Djobeïdj, cited by Ibn el Beïthar). Ho-
beïch ibn el Hassan, who also knows this test, remarks concerning
sunhang that it smells like a chamber pot or soiled clothing.

vetus parvæ virtutis est: The drug deteriorated and became dark.
Antiquum autem denigrat tempus (Mesuë). Compare also Avi-
cenna (II, 2, p. 105v).

abluatur: Strong preparations were washed out in water or women's milk
in order to weaken their effect. The rule was first to give mild medi-
caments, later the stronger ones (Galen, de comp. medic. local. s. sec.
loc. libri X, lib. II, cap. 2; Kühn XII p. 590). Compare also Ori-
basius II, p. 264. Washings with water and with crocus solutions
were used to detect adulterations of Aloe (Mesuë, l. c. f. XXXIIv).

ad comedendum: Aloe is given in the morning. The lower classes
take it in the evening and then sleep, but this is an error and
a mistake, since Aloe has no value after a meal (Ibn Serafioun, cited by
Ibn el Beïthar).

AGARICUS is Polyporus officinalis, Fr. (Boletus Laricis, Jacq.). Medieval
physicians were in doubt as to whether it was a fungus.
They distinguished between a male and a female variety. The former was
considered poisonous and was not used. Agaricus is not mentioned by
Harpestreng.

calidus in II, siccus in III: Avicenna states that Agaricus is
warm in the first degree and dry in the second (Canon. II. 2. p. 107v and De medic.
4*

52

cord. II p. 562v). Mesuë says the same, as does Constantinus Africanus (p. 346).

utramque coleram: It purges thick, putrid phlegm and yellow and black bile from the brain (Mesuë). By solution it draws out the coarser diverse humors of melancholy and phlegm and red choler (Avicenna II, 2, 108r). See also Galen: De simpl. med. facult. lib. VI (Kühn XI p. 813).

veneni: There is moreover in it a theriacal property against every poison. (Avicenna, De med. cord. II p. 562v. See also Galen, De simpl. med. fac. II and Oribas VI p. 427). The drug was also used against poisonous Bites and Stings and against harmful Influences of every kind. By this means it became a remedy for keeping Old Age at bay.

mortiferis: The belief in Agaricus' power as an antidote was so great that people carried the drug on their person as an amulet against Scorpion stings. (Ibn el Beïthar).

electuariis: The electuaries were used to attain eternal Youth. Aldobrandino of Siena writes (p. 81): And the electuaries one makes from mirabolans ten drams, [and of escaille de feer two drams] and of agaric two drams and mix together, and blend with honey and sugar and it will make an electuary. And this electuary, as we have said, whoever wishes to remain young should take it every day of the year, in the morning, fasting, and drink one cup of wine afterwards and should refrain from eating until midday, for these are things that above all things delay old age, as Avicenna says.

albus: The best Agaricus was light, white and brittle. The white Color gave occasion for it also being called cor album abietis. (Alphita).

dosis: In general the Authors give no Dose. (Avic., Oribas, Rhazes). Dioscorides gives 2–3 obols and 1–2 drachms, Constantinus Africanus gives as the only Dose mentioned, exagium unum.

ARMONIACUM is gum-resin ammoniacum, derived from Dorema ammoniacum, Don. Galen and Dioscorides considered the Plant to be a species of Ferula, and the latter states that the useful variety grew in Libya near Cyrene, while another, inferior variety originated from the Oasis of Jupiter Ammon. The drug's quality was determined by

53

The purity. It should be granular like frankincense, smell like castoreum, and taste bitter. As a test, it was dissolved in water; the solution should then be milk-white.

Ammoniacum in Harpestreng, see p. 86 and K. U², 2. The identity of the drug is probable, but not entirely certain.

calidum: It is warm at the end of the second degree and dry in the first (Avicenna II. 2. cap. 8); warm in the third degree, dry in the second (Constantinus Afric. p. 375).

ydropicis et spleneticis: Dioscorides describes its diuretic effect and states that the drug is good for the Liver and Spleen. It benefits those suffering from sciatica, gout, and arthritis caused by viscous phlegm. One drachm taken with oxymel cures diseases of the spleen (Constantinus Afric. p. 375).

paraliticis: Agaricus was a nerve remedy, used against Epilepsy and peripheral Neuralgias (Sciatica). For these latter conditions, Dioscorides used Liniments with Ammoniacum, Vinegar, Natron, and Cyprus oil.

arteticis: For gouty joint ailments, poultices of Ammoniacum with Honey or Tar were used.

ACUANUM. Avicenna gives (p. 173, cap. 712) information about what Acuanum is. The chapter is headed "De Uchuen," and in the margin it is noted that the plant is also called Achuan or Alachuan, "id est matricaria." Dioscorides deals with this plant in chapter 145 (155) under the name Parthenion, a designation which Pliny I, XXII, c. XVII uses for several different plants — Perdicium, Helxine, Linozostis, and Cichorium; it is probably this last name which through a misunderstanding became scorulo. Berendes notes in his Commentary on Dioscorides that some believe Parthenion is Matricaria Chamomilla, others that it is M. Parthenion. It is indeed altogether impossible to determine which of today's plants corresponded to Parthenion.

flegma: it is indeed taken dry in oxymel like epithymum, and it dissolves melancholy and phlegm. (Avicenna p. 173v).

cum oximelle: it was given dry with Oxymel and thereby purged Mucus and black Bile. (Dioscorides).

54

AQUA CASEI = serum lactis (Galen) = aqua lactis = Valle. The Greek physicians described Milk as consisting of Cheese, Whey, and Fat. The whey had a purging effect, especially when it had been separated by boiling. Various kinds of Milk were used; the most effective was Women's milk, followed by Goat's milk, Ass's milk, Ewe's milk, and Cow's milk. Mesuë does not mention the use of Women's milk (f. XXXIVr). Oribas gives detailed discussion of Milk's laxative effect (see e.g. I. 242, VI. 30).

coleram rubeam: this effect is generally noted, but since the remedy was itself weak in action, other purgatives were added, e.g.: Myrobalan, Rhubarb, Rose juice, Violet, Tamarind, Cassia fistula, Fumitory, and the like. (Mesuë).

nigram: with a solution of polypody it draws out melancholy and burnt humors (Mesuë).

aquam citrinam: Mesuë uses Asarum and Iris.

coleram adustam: By solution it draws out choler and burnt humors with ease and is beneficial against mania and melancholy (Mesuë).

ulceribus: And it is a good medicine for infections of the skin whose matter is choler and burnt humor, such as impetigo and dry ringworm, and pustules and itching and dry malignant ulcers and leprosy and similar conditions. (Mesuë). Its use against Wounds is discussed by Galen (De simpl. med. fac. X).

ABSINTHIUM = Arthemisia Absinthium, L., not to be confused with Dioscorides' ἀψίνθιον Θαλάσσιον, the Greeks' seriphon. The drug is discussed by Harpestreng (S. 6, K. U¹, 3).

calidum: warm in the first degree and dry in the second. (Constantinus Afric. p. 344).

multiplex: In antiquity the drug was obtained from many different places, and each variety had its own name. Dioscorides considered the Pontic and Tauric varieties the best. Avicenna (II, II, cap. 2) knows five kinds: its species are five, namely tarsense, susi, nabati, corasceni, and romanum. Apuleius names Egypt and Italy as its place of origin.

crocei coloris: The Arabs held differing opinions about the appearance of the plant. In Ibn el Beïthar, authors are cited (Chérif and Abou Obeid el Becry), of whom one holds that the flower is white on the out-

55

whitish and yellow inside, while the other describes it as yellow throughout.

lanuginem: Abou Djoreidj (in Ibn el Beïthar) knows several kinds of Absinthium, but the Syrian one from Taurus is the best. It is woolly and has small nodes like Satureja. However, it connects differently with the comparison to chickens and young doves than what is written, and Henricus Dacus' text is certainly due to an incorrect use or a misunderstanding of an Arabic text. Abou Djoreidj writes namely about the above-mentioned Syrian species, that it gives off, when crushed, "emanations similar to those of Socotrine aloes, whose yellow color resembles that of the down of young pigeons."

aloes: see the Note above. The comparison is also found in Avicenna (II, II, cap. 2).

nodi: these small nodes are mentioned by most Arabic authors.

virtutem habet: It strengthens the liver and opens its obstructions, stimulates appetite, and cures jaundice (Constantinus Afric. p. 345).

yctericiam: And it is useful for jaundice, especially if drunk for ten days, taking three ounces per day (Avic. II, II, cap. 2). Dioscorides also treats jaundice with a decoction or infusion of Absinthium.

sanguinem in venis: For this purpose Syrupus Absinthii was used (Avicenna). It drives out the bilious humors of the stomach through the lower passages, and evacuates them through the urine. Moreover, it purges through the urine what is bilious in the veins (Galen, De simpl. med. fac. VI; Kühn XI p. 844).

mundificat stomachum: Avicenna considered the juice harmful to the stomach on its own. He therefore gave syrups or extracts of the plant, or gave it combined with other drugs.

compositum cum epithimo: Hobeïch (in Ibn el Beïthar) recommends infusion and decoction given together with Epithimus for melancholic persons.

Bellerici are the fruits of Terminalia Bellirica, Roxb., of the Combretaceae family. The Arabic name for the drug was beliledj, derived from the Persian belileh.

frigidam: They are cold in the first degree, dry in the second (Avic. II, II, cap. 91).

56

similes: Avicenna compares it with Myrobalanus emblica, as does Mesuë. Ishak ibn Amran (according to Ibn el Beïthar) states that one may substitute the drug with an equal weight of myrob. emblica.

cum gallis: Avicenna (loc. cit.) writes: Bellyrici strengthen the stomach together with aldebag. This Arabic word is explained as follows in Andreae bellunensis's interpretatio Arabicorum nominum in libris Avicennae: Aldebach is a preparation or tanning process, and properly speaking a preparation of hides with galls and a kind of ink and other things, so that they become hard, compact, and resistant to hard and sharp things that would otherwise break them.

BDELLIUM is a gum resin, originating from the plant Commiphora (Balsamea) africana. Its Arabic name was Bdeliun, which is said to mean "the Lion's Rest." Galen (Kühn XI. 849) knew two forms: the Scythian, "which is indeed somewhat pungent and resinous, and quite emollient and efficacious"; and the other, the Arabic, "which is clearer and dries more than it softens." Later a further form was known, called opacum.

calidum et humidum: In the last part of this section, bdellium is described as "calidum et siccum," as the author has conflated the properties of the two forms. In Avicenna these are called iudaicum and mechium, and he writes (II, II, cap. 112) "mechium is cold and dry, the other is warm." Constantinus Africanus gives (p. 359) calidum in the second degree, humidum in the first.

emorroidis: Against hemorrhoids Avicenna uses Bdellium, partly as an internal medicine, partly as a poultice, and partly for fumigation. Its use is justified by the fact that the drug was regarded as a remedy against all kinds of swellings.

arteticis: Bdellium acts as a diuretic.

laxare: According to Ibn Massouih the drug was good to give together with strongly purging medicines, since it weakened their effect. It was used for intestinal disorders and ulcerations.

CENTAUREA = Centaurea Centaurium L. The name comes from the Centaur Chiron (Chiron centaurus has herbas fertur invenisse a quo tenet nomen centaurium (Apuleius)). A. distinguishes between C. maius and C. minus. Centaurium maius, called by some narcen, by others chtroniam,

57

Others call it Maroniam, Italians call it fel terrae (earth's gall), the Prophets call it Haema herculis. Centaurium minus: there are those who call it limnesium, others helleboriten, others amaranthum, the Magi call it Sanguinem herculis, the Dacians Tulbala, the Romans Febrifugiam, or multiradicem (the many-rooted herb) (see also Dioscorides). Alphita has the names limpnesia and fel terrae and for maius, marta and genciana. Harpestreng mentions Centaurea (S. 72. K. U¹ 34).

calida: warm and dry in the third degree (Avicenna II, II, c. 158). Constantinus Africanus (p. 367), however, assigns it a different degree.

subtilis: Galen also distinguished between Cent. maius and C. minus. Paulus Aeginetes considers the root of Cent. Centaurium to be astringent, whereas that of Erythraea Centaureum L. (minus) is ineffective. A decoction of its stalks, used as an enema, did however have a laxative effect (see Berendes' edition, Janus 1913 p. 26).

laxat: According to Dioscorides the plant should be boiled, and the decoction then acted as a purgative on bilious substances. (Dioscorides).

arteticis: It was C. minus that was used against gout (Galen), whose symptoms are noted by several of the Arabic authors.

sciaticis: The drug was regarded by the Arabic physicians as a specific remedy for nerve complaints. Ibn el Beithar lists a number of physicians who used it against convulsions, neuralgias, sciatica and the like. Avicenna mentions sciatica, nerve pains and nerve contusions. Constantinus Africanus records almost the same applications.

colicisque doloribus: If one drachm of it is given with wine, it relieves pain in the belly and stabbing pains caused by gross humors and flatulence (Constantinus Afric. p. 363).

decoctio: The decoction was used as a blood-cleansing enema (sciatica) (Diosc., Avic.).

coqui succus: The method of preparation is described by Dioscorides (III, 7 (9)).

CROCI ORTENSIS MEDULLA: The Middle Ages knew two forms of Crocus — the oriental Saffron on the one hand, and Crocus ortensis on the other, the so-called safran de cortil (see Platearius: Liber de simpl. medic. dictus circa instans). Botanically these plants are quite different, as the oriental Saffron consists of the stamens of Crocus sativus L., whereas Crocus ortensis is Carthamus tinctorius L. Of Carthamus it was known

58

According to Mesuë (l. c. f. XXXVIIIr) there are two varieties: domesticus and silvestris; the first was used, and its seed was considered the best. The flower was of lesser value: "the seed which is best is that which is white, flat, large and full, whose pith is unctuous and fatty, and whose bark is thin." It can thus be seen that the word medella recorded in the Register of the Text should rightly be read as medulla, a word that is also used in the Text itself.

The flower of Carthamus was considered best when it resembled Crocus; from a medical point of view, the drugs must have had roughly the same effect. Crocus hortensis is accordingly included in the preparation Esdra in the Antidotarium Nicolai, and in Platearius' Circa instans three notes are found on the use of Crocus hortensis, but only one on true Saffron. The drugs appear to have been used somewhat interchangeably, which may be connected partly with the fact that they could substitute for one another, and partly that Saffron had already been heavily adulterated in antiquity (see Dioscorides and Plinius I, XXI, c. XVII). Crocus is found in Harpestreng (S. 51, K. U¹, 30).

calida et sicca: hot and dry in the second degree (Constantinus Afric. p. 363).

purgat flegma: By dissolving, it expels phlegm through the bowels and by vomiting (Mesuë). The laxative effect is also mentioned by Oribas (II 259, 260, see also II 548). According to Dioscorides (IV 187) it cleansed, but was harmful to the stomach.

ipozarcam: Carthamus removed accumulations of fluid in the body (Mesuë) and was used against Ascites and Anasarca.

colicam: Carthamus cleansed away mucus and bile. The juice was pressed out of the crushed seeds and the preparation was given in chicken broth together with other remedies. (See Constantinus Afric. p. 363 and Oribas II 122–123).

Sale indico: Sal indicum [Sodium chloride / rock salt] is one of the four kinds of salt described by Constantinus Afric. (p. 387). Its "color belongs to blackness, yet it is bright and hard."

CASSIA FISTULA = Cassia fistula L. The designation fistula was first applied to a bark that was rolled together like a tube in the same manner as Cinnamon, to which it was compared. (Galen

59

Concerning antidotes I, cap. 14; Kühn XIV, p. 69). This bark had nothing to do with Cassia fistula; the latter was, as Arabic authors repeatedly note, unknown to Galen and Dioscorides. The plant's external appearance was first described by Abul Abbâs Annâbati of Seville at the beginning of the 13th century, while Johannes Actuarius described the fruit somewhat later. In the therapeutics of the Salerno school, Cassia was a widely used medicine. The plant was cultivated especially in Egypt and was already exported from there in the early Middle Ages. Harpestreng has Cassia (S. 64, K. U¹ 32).

calida et humida est, purgat . . .: it is moist in the first degree and is soothing, dissolving, and clarifying of the blood, sedating its sharpness, and [good] against red bile (Mesué). Constantinus Afric. considers it mediocre between hot and dry.

laxat suaviter: the laxative effect is mentioned by most Arabic authors; this led to the drug being used against liver diseases.

coleram purgat: It has been noted above that Cassia cleansed red bile, which Constantinus Afric. (p. 347) also states. It was also used by medieval physicians against black bile (Aldobrando p. 46), and was thus also a remedy against melancholy.

sed uirtutem: it is hinted that Cassia caused colic when used in patients with weak bowels.

cum tamarindis it acted as a bile-driving agent (see Ibn el Beïthar). After choleram the word nigram should therefore be added.

tercianis: It does not appear to have been a particularly specific remedy for tertian fever, since it is generally cited as useful against hot fevers (Mesué et al.). According to the liber experiencium (in Ibn el Beïthar) one could give Cassia in whatever fever period one wished.

solatrum = Solanum nigrum L. It is also called morella or strignum.

coriander is already mentioned in the Papyrus Ebers. The plant gives off an unpleasant smell, which led people in the Middle Ages to consider it poisonous. The smell is not found in the ripe fruits, which were used early on, in part as a flavor corrective.

apostema: it benefits hot swellings in the internal organs and particularly the throat when a gargle is made from it with water of solatrum, and it is applied

60

against hard apostemes and it benefits them (Avicenna II, II, 121). Mesue says it "soothes the chest and throat and resolves acute apostemes in them" (see also Constantinus Africanus).

melior est: There were two varieties. Avicenna (II, II, p. 121) calls them kebulica and aegyptiaca. Ibn Djoldjol (in Ibn el Beithar) gives their homelands as Egypt and Iraq. The medicament was obtained from a hard, black tube, which was the fruit. This was internally divided into chambers, in which was found a black, honey-like pulp that stuck to the fingers and at the same time tasted both sweet and sour. Melior est illa quae sumitur a canna et quae splendidior et pingvior. (Avic. l. c.).

CUCUMERES AGRESTES: Dioscorides (IV, 152) lists a large number of names for the plant called wild Sikys, whose Greek name was Elaterion (= purgative). The Romans called it Cucumis rusticus, agrestis, anguinus, or silvestris, while the Arabs used the designation Cucumis asininus. According to Dioscorides it resembles the cultivated cucumber, from which it differs in that the fruit is much smaller and resembles an elongated acorn, as Pliny (I. XX. c. I–III) and the Arabic authors (Mesue and others) also note. The plant's current name is Momordica elaterium, L. Both the fruit and the root were used, but the former was the most powerfully active. The drug is not mentioned in Harpestreng.

calide: in the third degree (Avicenna II, II, 177; Mesue), in the second (Oribas II, 685).

arteticis: Avicenna uses a decoction of the drug as a clyster for gouty complaints. It was used in a plaster prepared with vinegar for podagra (Dioscorides, Avicenna).

emigraneis: The juice was used against migraine. The drug was in general a nerve remedy (see Galen: De simpl. med. facult. VIII; Kühn XII p. 122). Hobeich (in Ibn el Beithar) used it against facial tic.

paraliticis: The drug was included in the Pillulae diacastoreae in the Antidotarium of Nicolaus, of which it is said "prosunt paralysi."

occasu pleiadum: The rising of the constellation of the Pleiades in the sky in the middle of the month of May was regarded as a sign that the harvest season was about to begin and that navigation was opening. Their setting at the begin-

61

The end of November was a sign for the new sowing and also that shipping came to a halt on account of the autumn storms.

hic tempus: The end of summer was the right time for harvesting the fruit (Avic., Mesue); the root, on the other hand, was to be gathered in spring.

citrinis: The yellow colour was the sign of ripeness. Furthermore, the fruit was to detach itself from the stalk at the slightest touch of the hand, and the seeds were to spring out.

melior: The best one is that which is yellow, straight like a cucumber, of genuine bitterness; and the best juice is that which is white, flat, and smooth, resembling the squill onion, and over which a full year has already passed (Avicenna II, II, 177).

exprimi: The extraction of the juice is described by Avicenna (II, II, 177). "He takes the fruit ... and it is suspended in a cloth so that its water runs out, and it is strained and dried in a dish over ashes, and placed on a board in the shade." The juice was not to be pressed out. Mesue states: the extraction of the juice should be carried out with ease, not by laborious compression.

trociscos: Avicenna has (V, S. I, Tr. VIII p. 543v) a preparation of this kind. It is called "Trochisci conferentes ad febres antiquas et inflammationem et vomitum, et leniunt naturam" [lozenges effective against chronic fevers, inflammation, and vomiting, and they soothe the constitution].

anni: The efficacy of the juice diminished upon standing. The remedy would "become tempered."

frangere virtutem: The drug was also tempered with almond gum. There were moreover specific rules governing which drugs might be combined with Cucumis agrestis. If pills were made, one was not to use the warming purgatives, such as Scammonea and Colocynth, since these would thereby produce an excessively violent effect. They could, however, be used to good advantage in electuaries.

gumma senisorum = g. sarazenorum = g. arabicum.

COLOQUINTIDUM = Citrullus Colocynthis, Schrader, (Cucumis Colocynthis L.).

calidum: It is commonly given as the 3rd degree of heat (Avicenna II, II, 127; Mesue).

a cerebro: Avicenna states that it purges the brain. For the

62

Arab physicians regarded it in general as a nerve remedy, given for headache, meningeal disorders, convulsions, migraine, epilepsy, paralysis, minor cramps, sciatica and the like (see Ibn el Beïthar).

ascendere: Colocynth cleansed the body of thick, slimy fluids that penetrated throughout the body and also sent their vapors up to the head, as well as the harmful humors that derived from black bile (Hobeïch).

a profundo: This effect is mentioned in several places among the Arab authors. Mesüë cites the following statement by Hunain: "By dissolution it draws out phlegm and viscous humors, pulling them from the depths of the limbs."

crocei coloris: The fruit of colocynth is green, but turns brown when dried. The pulp contained in the fruit is yellowish-white or entirely white. Avicenna (II, II, 127), who distinguishes between the two sexes of the plant, gives the following rules for the collection of the drug: That which is to be selected from it should be white, of intense whiteness and smooth; for that which is black among them is bad and the hard one is bad. And it is necessary that when it is gathered, its pulp should not be removed from its interior: rather let it remain within it as it is: it is not weakened if this is done, and let it not be gathered until it begins to turn yellow: and let not the green color be stripped from it entirely: and if not, then it itself is harmful and bad. And some have said it is necessary that its rind and seed be separated from it. And when there is not more than one colocynth on the tree, it is harmful. And indeed the male hairy one is stronger than the loose female. The plant itself was also regarded as poisonous, not only when it bore but a single fruit. Mesüë writes accordingly that it kills all plants in its vicinity. It was therefore also called "nex plantarum" (slayer of plants), and the ground in which it grew and over which it cast its shadow looked as though it had been scorched. The Arabs considered the female plant the best, as it had a weaker effect than the male plant.

occasu pleiadis: see the note on p. 60 below.

vomitum facit: That which is gathered while green loosens superfluously and causes excessive vomiting and disturbs to such a degree that it may perhaps kill (Avicenna, l. c. p. 114).

estu: Colocynth should not be given either when it was very cold or very warm. If given during great heat, it was harmful

63

for the stomach and anus, since one risked bleeding due to the drug's irritating effect. If it was very cold, it caused colic and stomach cramps without evacuation (Hobeïch). Dioscorides (IV, 175) mentions bloody diarrheas.

extra suum corticem: The pulp quickly lost its potency when removed from the fruit. If allowed to remain in its natural casing, it could keep for a long time (Abou Djoreidj in Ibn el Beïthar). Et cum extrahitur pulpa eius tempus debilitat eam (Mesuë) [And when the pulp is extracted, time weakens it].

frangatur: Before gum arabic was added, the pulp was freed from the shell and seeds. Tragacanth or starch was also used to weaken the effect. The pulp was to be finely divided and completely free of shell and seeds, since it was believed that pieces of these could lodge in the intestines and cause violent diarrheas; "et excoriatur vias" (Mesuë) [and they would abrade the passages].

DIAGRIDIUM. Diagridium or Diagrydium (δακρὺδίον = tear) is a medieval term for scammonea, the gum resin of Convolvulus Scammonea, L. It was obtained either by cutting off the top of the root, hollowing it out, and letting the resin collect in the bowl-shaped hollow, or by letting the resin flow out through deep incisions in the root. The drug is an ancient remedy, mentioned repeatedly by Hippocrates, who used it as a purgative in fevers, as a diuretic, in gynecology and obstetrics. Scammonea is mentioned in Harpestreng (p. 87[?], 121 and K. U² 43).

colorem album: Dioscorides (IV, 168) considers the best kind to be translucent, light, the color of ox-gall, and perforated with fine channels like a sponge. Hobeïch states that the color should have a bluish tinge.

Antiochia: This city is cited as the place of origin by el Madjoussy. The plant was moreover widespread over large parts of Arabia, Armenia, Turkey, Asia Minor, and Syria.

eius species: When the body's fluids became corrupted, they were thought to take on colors that were variations of the original (see Cantica Avicennæ p. 507v). Some of these were regarded as particularly harmful. Reflections of this kind had already been put forward by Galen in

64

On the differences of diseases, but these were developed further by the Arabs and the men of the Salerno school.

forti virtute: It harms the liver and stomach, and suppresses appetite (Constantinus Africanus). Arab medicine regarded it as established, however, that an incorrect preparation of the drug could cause it to act too violently.

turbacionem: For indeed a biting flatulence in the stomach produces disruption, nausea, and troublesome agitation (Mesue).

excoriationem refers to the bloody diarrhea that the remedy could bring about.

frangitur: The too powerful effect had to be corrected with other remedies and through the indications for its use. "Therefore the ancients added to it anise, carrot, and parsley to be mixed, and ground with almond or cooked in quince preparations" (Constantinus Africanus, p. 369). Precisely because of the danger of bloody diarrhea, Diagridium was considered harmful to the stomach and was therefore not used in cases of ventricular ailments, states of debility, or during fever. Correction was achieved by adding "strengthening" remedies (Aloe and Mastic) for the cold natures, while the warm ones received preparations to which rose extract or quince syrup was added.

Regarding the aforementioned Aloe, cited by several authors, it must nonetheless be said that Oribas (II 123, V, 27, 28) firmly protests against mixing Aloe, Thyme, and Salt with Diagridium, precisely because of the ventricular conditions.

pomorum: Mesue also uses cooking in hollowed-out apples; more commonly used were quinces, which were considered astringent and which reduced the drug's ability to penetrate (Mesue). Quinces belonged to the "compressiva."

The preparation was carried out as follows: one took a quince and cut off one end, so that the removed piece formed a lid. The interior was hollowed out and filled with scammony, after which the lid was fitted precisely back on, fastened with a wooden peg, and the opening sealed with dough. The quince was then placed in the oven on a brick, after the fire had gone out. It was left to stand until the contents began to boil; it was then opened and the preparation removed. It was thereafter dried in the shade (Hobeich). The preparation could keep for a very

65

For a long time, when it had been prepared in this manner, it would otherwise quickly deteriorate. There were moreover several preparation methods; the one mentioned above agrees almost entirely with that given by Oribasius (II p. 267).

Similiter: Concerning Aloe, see the note frangitur, last section. Mesué (f. XXXVIv) gives the following method as deriving from Rufus: Scammony is to be boiled in quince after it has been wrapped and rolled for approximately one day with violet oil or rose oil or almond oil; after that it is to be rubbed gently and rolled and dissolved in a glass dish until it dries, with an infusion of citrine myrobalans made in quince juice.

Confectionibus: Scammony is found in several preparations in the Antidotarium of Nicolai. (cf. for example Diaprunis).

minoris malicie: For this purpose, its cooking helps us along with those things that extinguish and soothe, such as mucilage of psyllium and water and the flesh of plums and juice of roses and water of violets and fresh violets. And wrapping it before its decoction in rose oil or violet oil removes this harmful effect from it. And the juice of quinces, mulberries, sumac, and spodium act similarly (Mesué).

Epithimum is Cuscuta Epithymum, L. The name suggests that the plant is often found in the shade of, or together with, Thyme. According to Dioscorides it was native to Cappadocia and Pamphylia.

calidum: Avicenna, citing Galen, places it in the third degree. He also cites Hunain, who gives it as warm in the third degree, dry at the end of the first. Constantinus Africanus p. 368 gives it as warm and dry in the middle of the third.

coleram nigram: Epithymum was a principal remedy against Melancholy. Hobeïch notes, however, that if the drug is given to bilious persons, it worsens their constitution, and its use causes discomfort and vomiting.

coleram rubeam: It disturbs those in whose constitutions red bile predominates, and causes them nausea (Avicenna. II, II, 225).

senibus: It calms flatulence, and is suitable for those of firm constitution and for the elderly, and it removes the melancholy of illness (Avic. l. c.). Besides the elderly, Hobeïch also mentions thin persons.

melancholia: Dioscorides (IV, 176) calls Epithymum a speci-
5

66

proven remedy against Melancholy. It has the prerogative of drawing out melancholy above all other purging agents (Mesue f. XXXVr). If indeed 10 drachms of epithyme powder in a thin, loosely woven cloth are steeped in sweet wine from the first hour of night until dawn, and the cloth is then pressed out and the liquid drunk together with a little violet or almond syrup, it is most beneficial for melancholics (Constantinus Afric. p. 368).

laudabilius: The red, sweet-smelling Epithymum came from Crete. That which was less red came from Syria and was of lesser rank. Avicenna also knows of a variety that came from Jerusalem. The redder and more fragrant it was, the better.

depone ab igne: The drug lost its potency through boiling, which is why, as indicated in the following directions, Epithymum was added last.

non indiget rectificationem: Epithymum was used as a corrective addition to other drugs. To moderate its effect, it was given in almond oil, or one was content simply to crush it or to pull it apart coarsely.

ELLEBORUS ALBUS. It has until now proven impossible to identify the plant that in Antiquity and the Middle Ages was called Helleborus albus, since the genera Melampodium, Helleborus, and Veratrum were lumped together. For Galen there is accordingly no difference in the effect of white and black Helleborus, even though they differ in taste. Alphita states: Elleborus, when used without qualification, is understood to be white, and here Elleborus albus is equated with veratrum.

Eleborus is mentioned in Harpestreng (p. 120. K. U2, 21).

calidus: The text follows here Constantinus Afric. (p. 371). Avicenna (II, II, 238) has in medio tertii.

laudabilior: Dioscorides recommends the white variety, which is brittle, whose fracture has not been walked upon, and which has a white pith. The taste should not be particularly burning and should not cause excessive salivation.

proprietas: Its effect was to cleanse humor viscosus et mucosus. (Badighoras in Ibn el Beithar).

vomitum: Avicenna gives a detailed account of its toxic effects. Its use can cause convulsions, and death can follow from misuse. Elleborus albus is a poison for dogs and pigs, and even the excrement of persons who have taken it can kill

67

Hens and Quails. Elleborus albus was used quite extensively by the Hippocratic physicians (De salubr. diæta 5. De int. aff. 7.), who nevertheless feared its toxic effects and therefore only administered it together with other remedies in cases where one wished to induce vomiting. The Arabic physicians also weakened the drug before use. They would macerate the plant for three days in rainwater, then boil it down to one third and decant it. The plant material was discarded, the water mixed with honey, and the mixture heated until it reached the consistency of syrup.

ELLEBORUS NIGER: King Proitos's daughters of Argus were cured of their madness by the physician Melampus, who gave them Helleborus. The plant was named after him (Melampodion), but the plant can hardly be identified with certainty today. The choice lies principally between H. niger, H.
