Orientalis and Veratrum nigrum L., whose root contains very powerfully acting purgative substances. It was the peeled root that the ancient physicians used. The suggestion that Elleborus niger should be identified with H. orientalis is supported by the fact that the latter's root can be peeled, whereas the root of Helleborus niger in the modern sense cannot. The plant was considered highly poisonous. Those who gathered it protected themselves against the poison by eating onions and drinking wine.
calidus et siccus in III: Constantinus Afric. says the same. Avicenna (II, II, 237) has usque ad tertium.
laudabilior: Dioscorides (IV, 149) recommends the fleshy, strong, finely-pithed variety, which has a sharp and burning taste. The drug from Helikon was best, that from Antikyra, Parnas and Oeta inferior. According to Avicenna, the best is neither old nor new, of medium thickness, yellow in color, and breaks easily. In the hollow of the root there is a fine network, like a spider's web. The taste is sharp and burning.
desipientie: Dioscorides recommends Helleborus for raving madness. Mesué and Constantinus Afric. use it for both brain and nervous diseases. The former writes: "Est ex rebus solennibus in mundificando cerebrum," and mentions Hemicranium, Mania, Melancholy, Vertigo, Epilepsy and Paralysis.
morpheas: Dioscorides uses it against itch, Avicenna i
5*

68

Vinegar compresses against skin disease (morphea = leprosy?) and warts. In Mesue it is described as being like theriac and a sovereign medicine against leprosy, cancer, and varieties of herpes. Constantinus Africanus (p. 371) states it cures morphea, impetigo, and scabies.

rectificatur: The overly strong effect was reduced in a number of different ways, partly through the preparation of the drug, and partly by the addition of other substances. (See Mesue f. XLIr).

EUPHORBIUM is the resin of Euphorbia resinifera, Berg. The plant takes its name from Euphorbus, the physician of King Juba II (30 B.C.–24 A.D.), who first made use of it. He cured the king, who then wrote a book about the plant (Pliny XXV, c. VII). Its homeland is Morocco, as most ancient authors state. In Alphita and Hortus sanitatis, India is given. The drug was considered poisonous, and was therefore collected by tying sheepskins tightly around the plant, and then shooting arrows or throwing spears into it from a distance, whereby the milky sap immediately flowed out. The sap that ran down into the sheepskins was the purest; what fell on the ground was impure. In the Middle Ages it was believed that the flowing sap could kill people by its smell alone, and so collectors kept their distance during harvesting (Hortus Sanitatis). It also killed nearby plants, which is why it grew in isolation.

calidum: The same is stated by Constantinus Africanus (p. 381).

acuminis: Dioscorides (III, 86) reports that the taste was so burning and persistent that everything afterwards tasted of Euphorbium.

Laudabilius: The properties described here are commonly mentioned by the authors. The smell was so sharp that those who collected the drug had to cover their mouths and nostrils. Over the course of three to four years it lost its potency and became pale and difficult to dissolve in oil. It could, however, be kept potent by storing it in a vessel with peeled beans. (See also Mesue).

juncturis: By dissolution it draws out thick and viscous phlegm from the deep parts of the body, cleansing the hollow spaces of the joints of humors that are difficult to eradicate (Mesue). Ibn Massouih (according to Ibn el Beithar) writes that Euphorbium removes phlegm that lodges itself in the joints, the loins, and the intestines.

69

paraliticis: Dissolved in oil for rubbing in (Avicenna II, II, 232).
sciaticis: Dioscorides (and Constantinus Africanus) recommend Euphor-
bium in an aromatic solution against sciatica (see also Avicenna loc. cit.).
exhibetur: namely on account of its sharp taste and toxic
effect; it was mixed with honey or various eye-salves
(Dioscorides). If Euphorbium was given alone, a dose of 3 drachms
was fatal after 3 days' course, due to stomach and intestinal ulceration.
The purification process is mentioned in Oribas (II 121, 122), and in Mesüë (f.
XXXIX v) a series of methods is listed that rely on the Arabic
authors.

EPATORIUM = Agrimonia Eupatoria, L. (Eupatorium vulgare, Matth.
Dod.). According to Pliny (I, XXV, 6) the plant received its name from
King Mithridates Eupator, who is said to have been the first to use it. Others
connect the name with the plant's use against liver
diseases. (Galen, Paulus Aegineta). It is mentioned in Harpestreng
(p. 33. K. U¹, 36).
calidum est et siccum: hot in the first degree, dry in the second
(Avicenna (II, II, 239), Mesüë (f. XXXIV v), Constantinus Africanus p. 346).
melancholiam intestinorum: The plant cleansed against liver obstruction
(Galen). It helps with pains of the liver and its obstructions, and
strengthens it, and helps with hardness of the spleen and abscesses of the liver
and abscesses of the stomach. (Avicenna). It relieves pain of the liver,
dissolves its hardness, and opens its obstructions (Constantinus Africanus).
febres cronicas: It was given here with juice of wormwood. Mesüë
calls Eupatorium a good medicine for quartan fever and prolonged fevers.
Constantinus Africanus, using Dioscorides as his source, says it cures
long-lasting fevers, especially quartan fevers.
azarebatara = Asara bacchara, the plant Asarum europaeum, L.

ESULA = Euphorbia Esula, L., with the Arabic name Alsebra. The root-
bark was used.
calida est: Hunain considers it hot in degree II, dry at the end of III,
while Mesüë (f. XL r) rates Esula as warm and dry at the beginning
of degree III. Avicenna (II, II, 666) sides with Hunain, but writes

70

Concerning the milk-sap: Its milk is the last in both together, indeed in the fourth degree.

Sharpness and astringency: In it there are astringency and sharpness and rupture of the openings of the veins (Avicenna). In general, however, these properties were attributed to the milk-sap: its milk is hot: and it is composed of a sharp and subtle fiery substance and of an astringent earthy substance (Mesue).

The better kind: Two varieties were found: one is large, having round and thick roots, and of thick bark, dense and heavy. And another is small, having slender roots, and is of thin bark (Mesue). Avicenna (loc. cit.) writes: That which is better is smooth, tending toward redness, like rolled skin, having a fine bark, and that which has two reeds and is of light flesh and somewhat reddish and hard and that which is like a thread is bad, and the Persian kind is bad, and one ought not administer anything of it.

It dissolves yellow water: In solution it strongly draws out phlegm and yellow water and melancholic humors, and materials from the joints, and it helps with pains of these. And it is among the great medicines for dropsy. Yet it harms the liver and dries the body of the user. (Mesue).

Its milk: Mesue writes about Esula: It consumes semen, its milk does this more powerfully, and Avicenna urgently discouraged using the milk-sap: In the milk of this plant there is no goodness, and it does not seem to me that it should be given as a drink.

Harmful properties: Besides the above-mentioned harmful effects on the Heart, Liver, and Stomach, Esula also had the property of being able to cause bloody diarrheas (it excoriates the viscera, Mesue). The remedy was therefore rectified by the addition of cordial, hepatic, and stomachic medicines.

Infusion: The described method seems to derive from Rufus. Avicenna gives a slightly modified procedure: It is steeped whole in freshly milked milk, day and night, and this is renewed many times, and it is that which weakens and destroys its action in bad humors.

In the shade: The rules for which drugs should be dried in the Sun and which in the Shade are found in the Saladini de Esculo compendium

71

aromatariorum. Herbs and fine roots with thin bark were dried in the shade, seeds and large, coarse roots in the sun.

da cum: its excessively laxative effect was reduced by adding tragacanth, gum, bdellium, and the like.

in aquam solatri: the solutions mentioned above acted as refrigerants (Mesué).

trociscos: Let it be steeped in the juice of endive, fennel, and nightshade for three days, then dried out, and from this let lozenges be made with a moderate amount of Indian salt, turbith, and myrobalans or aloes, and it will be of strong benefit (Avicenna).

ponderis 1 dram: A weight of 2 drams of it is fatal (Avicenna).


FUMUS TERRE = Fumaria officinalis, L. The name derives from the fact that the eyes fill with tears, as from smoke, when the plant's juice is dripped into them. The Greeks' name for the plant was capnos or capnios. It is mentioned in Harpestreng (S. 82, K. U², 22).

frigidus est et siccus: cold in the first degree, dry in the second (Avicenna II. II. 275).

calorem a stomacho: A certain common person was accustomed to use it to strengthen the stomach and at the same time to lubricate the bowels (Galen, De simpl. med. fac., VII, Kuhn XII p. 9). It dries and benefits the stomach because it has considerable astringency and does not have a great quantity of obvious heat but its dryness is in the second degree. (Rhazes II, 448). It strengthens the stomach and opens obstructions of the liver (Avicenna; see also Constantinus Afric. p. 351).

prurigini et scabiei: It is taken as a drink for itching and scabies (Avicenna II, II, 275). As a skin remedy, Constantinus Afric. uses the raw juice; a watery maceration of the plant was used against lice and tinea, and against mange, an earth-smoke preparation was used partly in bathwater with added henna, and partly combined with tamarind.

humoribus venenosis et adustis: It draws out choleric and burnt humors, and its virtue extends to the veins, purifies the blood, and clarifies it (Mesué f. XXXIVv.). It purifies the blood (Avicenna). It purges burnt choler and clarifies the blood, especially when mixed with myrobalans (Constantinus Afric. l. c.).

72

Libra: Avicenna: the drink of it should be from a weight of 5 drams times ten up to 5 pounds, and up to two thirds of a pound with sugar, and of that which is dry, with medicines in decoction up to 5 drams times ten, and of the ground form as it is, from three up to seven. Mesue's doses are nearly the same. Ibn Massouih indicates, however, that the dose of the decoction is 5–6 drams; in substance 3–7 drams are given with the same quantity of Myrobalanus citr. The dose of the raw uncooked juice is 4–8 ounces with 7–8 ounces of Myrobalan and 10 drams of white sugar.

GRANATA. The pomegranate, the fruit of Punica Granatum, L., is known from the Bible and is often depicted on Assyrian sculptures. The tree was native to northwest India, Persia, Palestine, and Asia Minor, but was brought early to southern Italy, and by the 3rd century after Christ it was common there. Dioscorides distinguishes — as does Oribas, II 681 — between two kinds (sweet and sour pomegranate), but notes that both are beneficial for the stomach. He attributes to them, however, a slightly different action. The Arabs also know two varieties, but held that the seeds of Granatum muzum (the bitter-sweet) were harmful to the stomach. The two fruits also differed in quality. Avicenna (II, II, 313) says: that which is sweet is cold in the first degree and moist in itself, and the sour is cold and dry in the second degree. Ancient medicine used partly the rind of the fruit and partly the bark of the root as a drug. The latter, which Henricus de Dacia also uses, was employed on account of its astringent property and because it acted as a laxative. The root bark was used against tapeworm. Hortus sanitatis attributes the same action to the rind and the flower. Oribas considers the juice the weakest, the seeds stronger, and the rind of the fruit the strongest. The flowers correspond to this last in action.

It purges red bile: The sour kind suppresses bile and prevents the flow of superfluities to the internal organs, and specifically its juice does so, and in all its forms, so that even in the sour there is a cleansing with astringency..... The sweet pomegranate benefits inflammation of the stomach. And the sweet is suitable for the stomach because of that which is in it of subtle astringency. (Avicenna, loc. cit.).

73

On feverish heat: Pomegranate juice is beneficial for acute fevers and inflammation of the stomach, but the sweet variety often harms those who have acute fevers (Avicenna).

HERMODACTYLI. To this day it is hardly possible to identify from which plant the bulbs originated that, under the name Hermodactylus, enjoyed such great esteem in antiquity. They were exported from the Levant to the Mediterranean lands, where they found a new home. The bulbs exported from there to the rest of Europe were certainly of various species, but little by little Hermodactylus came to denote the bulbs of Colchicum variegatum, L., which grows precisely in the places mentioned. The name means Hermes' Fingers, a designation grounded in the bulb's resemblance in shape to a finger joint. Hermodactylus, mentioned by Alexander of Tralles (525–605) and Paulus of Aegina, was used early on as a purgative with harmful effects on the stomach. Colchicum was feared as harmful by physicians of antiquity. Dioscorides mentions a Colchicum generally considered to be C. autumnale, while his Ephemeron was probably a Convallaria. Various authors regard Iris tuberosa as having been Hermodactylus.

They are warm in nature: it is warm and dry, belonging to the second degree (Avicenna II, II, 343); Mesuë likewise calls it warm and dry in the first degree; but Constantinus Africanus (379) places it warm and dry in the third degree.

On joints: Mesuë: by dissolution it draws out thick phlegm from the joints properly. And it is a great medicine for arthritis and for gout. Avicenna: it benefits gout and immediately relieves pain in the manner of a plaster applied over the affected area. Constantinus Africanus: it cures pains of the joints, gout, and sciatica.

More praiseworthy qualities: According to Mesuë, Avicenna, and other Arabic authors, Hermodactylus was partly red, partly white, partly black. Of these, the red and the black were considered harmful. The requirements for quality are as stated by Henricus de Dacia. Avicenna (II, II, 343): The white one is better, and the one that is hard on the outside for breaking. Mesuë also requires that it be grossus (large/coarse).

Hippocrates: Hermodactyli are not mentioned in Hippocrates, nor under other forms of the name, and in the books on

74

The epidemics have nothing resembling the place cited. See the following note under Mesuë.

nocent stomacho: The harmful influence on the stomach is frequently mentioned. Avicenna states: it is bad for the stomach, weakening it, and the red and black kinds retain dissolving medicines in the stomach and attract the greatest harm. Mesuë: It is hostile to the stomach, accumulating in it very many superfluities and generating in it gross flatulences; and this harm is removed from it by mixing with it cumin, mastic, and ginger. Constantinus Africanus (379): with their own property they dissolve thick and viscous humors, but are nonetheless irritating, because they cause constriction and pain in the stomach.

pinguedini corvino: Raven fat is not mentioned in either ancient or medieval medicine. It is therefore reasonable to suppose that there is a scribal error for cervinum (deer fat), which finds its confirmation in the fact that deer fat is recommended by Petrus Hispanus as a stomach-soothing remedy, and that he uses various other organic substances derived from the deer against liver, spleen, and intestinal ailments.

KEBULI (Arabic-Persian: Kabouli) are the fruits of Myrobalanus (Terminalia) Chebula, Gärtn. In the name there is said to lie an allusion to Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, from whose vicinity the drug was thought to come. This is confirmed by Ishak ibn Amban (in Ibn el Beïthar), who describes it as black, fatty, and of better flavor than the other Myrobalans. Constantinus Africanus indicates an Indian island, Cebula, as its place of origin.

frigidi et sicci: Several of the Arabic authors assign it to the first degree. Mesuë has cold in the first degree, dry in the second; Avicenna (II, II, 449) likewise.

choleram nigram: Constantinus Africanus says the same, and Kebuli was commonly regarded as purging the harmful fluids from the body, especially black bile. Ibn Semdjoun (in Ibn el Beïthar) disputed this, however, since black bile was cold and dry, which Kebuli also was. They could therefore not act upon one another. According to Rhazes they have only a slight effect on cholera nigra. Avicenna says of the Myrobalans that they all extinguish black bile and are beneficial to it.

75

comprimendo: Rhazes, Avicenna, and Constantinus Africanus, among others, mention the drying effect. This produced a constricting action.

coleram rubeam: The kebulini are viscous, they loosen red bile.
debilius: A comparison among the various Myrobalans is found in Avicenna (II, II, 449).
decoctione: The composition of the decoction is given by Hobeïch. (Prunus, Jujuba, and Sebesten).

MIRABOLANI, Greek μυροβάλανος, hence better called Myrobalani. Five varieties were known: 1. Myrobalani emblici (embrici), the Indians' amalaka or amala, the Arabs' amledj (emleg). The drug used was the fruit of Phyllanthus Emblica, a Euphorbiaceae. 2. Myrob. bellirici, Arabic beliledj, belileg, the fruit of Terminalia Bellica (bellirica), Roxb. 3. Myrob. chebuli, the fruit of Terminalia chebula, Retz. 4. Myrob. indi (nigri, Damasonii), which were the unripe fruits of the foregoing. 5. Myrob. citrini (lutei) of Terminalia citrina, Roxb., coming from Goa and being the most widely used. The name referred to the strongly yellow color the fresh ones had. When dried, they became darker, reddish-yellow. Avicenna (II, II 449) has a somewhat different account: Some of them are unripe citrini, and others are nigri from India, and those are the ones which are last to reach maturity and are the plumpest, and others are kebuli, which are the largest of all, and others are sinii, which are small and smooth.

How the various types of Myrobalan were actually related to one another was early a subject of much discussion. Some authors held that they all came from the same tree, and that citrini were the unripe fruits and indi the ripe ones. Others held that citrini were harvested first, chebuli at a second harvest, since the tree bore twice. Finally, some held that each variety came from its own tree.

frigidi et sicci: Avicenna considers all Myrobalans to be frigidi in the first degree, sicci in the second.

laxant: citrini loosen bile and somewhat phlegm (Avic.) Myrob. citr., by virtue of their own properties, strengthen the stomach and expel coarse superfluities. (Rhazes, 476, 825). The purging effect was attributed to the gum content (Costa ben Luca in Rhazes).

76

constringendo: Avicenna mentions this property only for Chebuli and Indi, but it is also noted for citrini by other Arabic authors (Massih, Masserdjouih in Ibn el Beithar).

in aqua fricentur: The general method of preparation was to steep the drug in water to make an extract, which was then drunk. Constantinus Africanus (345): if they are steeped in warm water, the water to be drunk will be strongly laxative. But if they are cooked over a fire, the water in which they are cooked will be less laxative. For fire removes the gummy quality. Costa ben Luca says the same.

MIRABOLANI INDI or nigri, see the previous section.
laxant coleram nigram: And the nigri dissolve melancholy and are beneficial for hemorrhoids (Avicenna II, II 449).

virtus indorum: The Indi are of lesser coldness than Kebuli (Avic.).
solvunt enim stomacho: Indi fried in oil have a binding effect on the stomach (Avic.).

POLYPODIUM is Polypodium vulgare, L., or quercinum as it is also called, since it grows frequently on oak trees, which was thought to make it more potent than polypodies found elsewhere. Its roots were compared to the suckers of a cuttlefish, hence the name. (Diosc. Plin. I, XXVI, c. VIII). The Arabic name is bulubudiun or besbaig (besbag), still used in Morocco.

calidum: Avicenna (II, II, 535) rates it as warm in the second degree, dry in the third, at the extreme of drying. Mesue, Constantinus Africanus (368), and several others rate it as warm in the third degree, dry in the second.

melancoliam: By its dissolving action it relieves melancholy without irritation, and dissolves phlegm and watery humor (Avic.). By dissolving it expels black bile with ease, and thick and slimy phlegm, and the matter of the joints, and aids in colic according to every mode of its administration (Mesue). The drug was given alone, with sugar, or mixed into decoctions and electuaries; for palatability also as a powder mixed into food.

melius: The best of it is that which is large like a ring, tending toward green and citrine in color, solid and fresh, in which there is a hidden bitterness and a good flavor combined with astringency, and in its flavor is the taste of cloves (Avicenna). Mesue requires that it be knobbly. His indications of color differ from Avicenna's.

77

viride: Dioscorides mentions the green color that appears when the drug is scraped.

cum datur debet teri: If the drug was given together with a decoction or in wine, no corrective was needed. It was grated and mixed in.

epithimi: This preparation was given especially for liver and spleen diseases. Furthermore, Epithymus was thought to have the same but weaker effects as Polypodium. They could therefore partly substitute for one another.

exizacria: read as oxysaccharo. Sugar is believed to have been discovered by the Indians. Its refining is credited to the Persians. The Arabs brought sugar to the lands around the Mediterranean. It reached Venice in 996, but it was not until the Crusades, which began 100 years later, that the substance became common. Pliny (I, XII c. VIII) knew sugar as "ad medicinae tantum usus" (for medicinal use only). Oxysacchara seems to belong to Arabic medicine. Rhazes uses Oxymel and Oxysaccharum freely, and these were prepared by treating Honey and Sugar respectively with Vinegar.

cum brodio caulium uel galli veteris: The taste was masked by giving Polypodium in chicken broth or other decoctions, after which other medicines were added (fennel, ginger, etc.) (Dioscorides, Avicenna, Mesué). Pliny says that Polypodium burdens the stomach, and the idea that the drug was poisonous occasionally appears among the Arabs.

REUBARBARUM. In Dioscorides (III, 2) it is noted that the plant Rha, which others call Rheon or Rhian but which the Romans call Rhaponticum, grows in the regions beyond the Bosphorus, and he gives a description of this plant, which Pliny (I, XXVII, XII) also mentions in nearly the same way. He calls the plant Rhacoma. Rha is the river Volga, on whose banks the plant was found in the land beyond Pontus, where the Barbarians lived. (Rhaponticum, Rhabarbarum). The plant in question was Rheum Rhaponticum, L. (Polygonaceae). According to Berendes, people learned during the time of Mesué (it is not specified whether it was the elder Mesué (780–875) or the younger (11th century)), when Arab trade was at its height, a

78

originating from the lands near China, known as a strongly laxative root, and in the beginning both names were retained as being of the same meaning. When it became known in the 11th century that China was the home of the true rhubarb (Rheum palmatum, Rheum undulatum, L., Rheum officinale Baill.), the Greek authors (Stephanos, Magnetes, Nicolaus Myrepsos) gave it the name Rhabarber.

One learns about the Arab views on this drug from Ibn Djomaï's treatise on rhubarb, which is discussed in detail by Ibn el Beïthar. The name was used for four different kinds, of which three were genuine rhubarbs, being alike in their outward characteristics and having the same effects and properties. The fourth kind was entirely different from these three. Of the genuine rhubarbs, two were known under the name of old rhubarbs, in contrast to the third, the new one. Of the old rhubarbs, one was called rhubarb from China, the other rhubarb from Zendj. The new rhubarb was called Turkish or Persian rhubarb. The fourth originated from Syria.

The name old rhubarb thus encompassed two forms. One is mentioned by Dioscorides (III) and by Galen in Book VIII of De simpl. med. facult. (Kühn XII p. 112). This corresponds with Ibn Djomaï's rhubarb. The other kind is mentioned by Galen in De antidotis (Kühn XIV, 75), but Ibn Djomaï has not seen it in a reliable form.

calidum et est humidum: There was no agreement about the nature of the drug. Avicenna (II, II 578) does not mention it. Oribas (II, 495, 496, 679) writes that it contains something both cold and warm. Constantinus Afric. has calidum est siccum in secundo gradu, which Mesuë also states. Galen (VIII): habet enim quiddam terrestre frigidum, ceu indicio est adstrictio: et adiuncta est quædam caliditas, siquidem si plusculum mandatur, subacre conspicitur.

cassia fistula: Mesuë (f. XXXIIIv column 2) mentions the use of the two drugs together.

manna et tamarindi: The dosage is reduced, since the additives are also laxative.

colice: According to Ibn Djomaï, colics were caused by fecal accumulations, Pituita, or intestinal gas. Est conferens hepati et stoma-

79

cho and the weakening of both and their pains and internal pains and hiccups and ruptures and reduces the spleen (Avicenna). Dioscorides recommends it for use in bloating, spleen and liver diseases, stomach cramps and dysentery; Rhazes against apostema of the spleen and liver, for tetanus of the hypochondrium, for intestinal ulcers, for chronic flux of the bowels.

epar: see the above Note.

apostemata: See the note on colic under Rhazes. By apostema is understood an abscess, but also swellings of various kinds. Mesue uses apostemata virgae for condylomata. Albucasis has Pustulae ani = anal apostem = aldea alcohi = condylomata in ano, hemorrhoidal tumors. The meaning of apostemata in visceribus is uncertain.

REUPONTICUM, see the Introduction to Reubarbarum.

SCAMIA ERIS, read scoria eris, copper hammer-scale. By scoria or bactitura was understood the scales that were hammered off various metals, silver, iron, tin and copper, when they were forged. They were used most as drying agents for wounds and as caustics. Dioscorides considered the scales of Cyprian copper the best, while those derived from aes album (brass) were inferior, fine and weak. The Arabs did not entirely share these views. El Ghafeky (in Ibn el Beithar) also considers the reddish-yellow Cyprian the best, but also mentions a pure red and a dark red form, which are not used. Scoria ferri had been considered the strongest since the time of Galen.

The Arabian physicians knew that copper could cause poisoning; they therefore advised against preparing sour, sugary or fatty foods in copper vessels, and diseases were mentioned (elephantiasis, cancer, liver and spleen diseases) that one could contract by drinking from copper vessels. Scoria aeris was close to scoria ferri. Their effect was (Avicenna II, II 231) to strengthen the stomach and to dry it of excess fluid.

laxare flegmam et aquam: Avicenna states: it dissolves the citrine water when drunk with hydromel, and if the palate is rubbed with it, it excites

80

vomitum. The slag was given together with honey, or in the form of pills baked in flour. (Dioscorides).

hic: read hunc.

est: one or more lines have dropped out. The passage can possibly be completed as: Aes aliud est rubeum ad citrinitatem declinans . . . . quod est melius et aliud est rubeum clarum et alium rubeum ad nigredinem declinans et est genus aeris, quod dicitur talacon (Avicenna).

SEMEN URTICE. Galen (Kühn XI, 817) mentions only one Nettle, Acaleph, Urtica; Dioscorides mentions two, but the Arabs knew three species. El Ghafeky (in Ibn el Beïthar) lists them as follows: 1. A nettle with lentil-sized and lentil-shaped, green, shining, and hard seeds, round flower-clusters, and very long, invisible, loosely attached stinging hairs (Urtica pillulifera, L.), 2. The largest species, which has a reddish stem and whose seeds are the size of a mustard seed, and are bluish-white and flattened (Urtica dioica, L.), 3. A small, fine nettle with very small seeds (Urtica urens, L.). The identification of these nettles is certainly uncertain, and the existing interpretations (Berendes, Sprengel) do not agree. Pliny knows the nettle, and Harpestreng also mentions it (S. 7. K. U¹, 76). The seeds were commonly given in wine as an expectorant and diuretic. As a fast-acting laxative they were given in suppositories. As a tonic, the crushed seeds mixed with honey were used for rubbing on the penis. Galen considered the leaves more potent than the seeds.

calidum est: Urtica and its seed are hot in the third degree and dry in the second, but the seed is of lesser dryness than the plant itself (Avicenna II, II, 714).

solvit flegma: its seed purges viscous phlegm (Rhazes II, I, 21). According to Avicenna (II, II, 714), nettle cleanses the chest when drunk with barley water, and when the leaves are boiled in barley water they remove the gross humors from the chest. The seeds, however, are more powerfully effective and help against asthma, shortness of breath, and pleurisy. In suppositories, Urtica acted as a laxative; Galen states that it is mildly laxative: it draws down the bowels only by a kind of cleansing and, as it were, tickling, not by purging. In De aliment. facult. (II, c. 54) he writes

81

he states that Urtica should not be used as a food, but that it is good as a medicine, since it acts as a laxative. Oribas says the same (I, 81).

SENNA: Senna's Arabic name is Abalzemer. The drug is obtained from several different Cassia species (obovata, Colladon, lenitiva, Bischoff and angustifolia, Vahl); it is found in two forms, partly as foliola, partly as folliculi, both of which were previously imported from Alexandria and Tripolis. The medieval Arabic physicians knew both forms, but preferred to use the leaves. The fruit is known to have been known in Europe in the eighth century, while the leaves were not introduced until the eleventh. Senna was imported partly as Senné Oriental or Senné de Levant, partly as Italian or Florentine Senna, and was found among merchants in three qualities: 1. Senné de Seyde or Senné de la palte, named partly after the place of cultivation and partly after a duty (palte) paid to the Sultan for an export license, 2. Alexandrian or Tripolitan Senna, 3. the lowest grade, Senna from Mokka.

calida: It is warm at the beginning of the second degree, dry in the first; the leaves are warm in the first degree (Mesuë).

laxat: In solution it easily draws out burnt melancholy and choler; and it cleanses the brain, heart, liver, and spleen, and the sense organs and lungs, and aids their ailments, and opens obstructions of the viscera (Mesuë). Omeiya (in Ibn el Beïthar) notes that Senna acts in the depths of the organs.

utile est: Mesuë does not mention the effect on Gout, which Omeiya does.

Rasis: Senna is mentioned by Serapion the Elder (9th century), but does not appear to have been mentioned by either Rhazes or Avicenna.

valet scabiei: Ishak ibn Honeïn cites Paulus, who uses Senna against cracks in the skin of the hands, hair loss, lice, scabies, and boils.

olei amigdalarum: Mesuë gives several methods of rectification, which were used because it was believed that the drug harmed the stomach while at the same time strengthening the heart.

6

82

TURBIT. The name derives from the Arabic-Persian Turbed-tirbid. The drug used was the root of Ipomoea Turpethum, R. Brown, a plant native to the East Indies and Polynesia. It is mentioned by Arabic authors as coming from Iraq and Khorassan. Mesué describes both a wild-growing and a cultivated variety, and notes that it is found in white, yellow, and black forms. Constantinus Africanus (366) does not know the black variety and gives Syria and Arabia as its place of origin.

calidum: Mesué assigns it the third degree of heat; other Arabic authors assign the second.

purgat flegma: By solution it draws out phlegm in great quantity and dissolves something of the burnt humors to a small degree. (Avicenna II, II, 701). By solution it draws out phlegmatic humors that are thick and viscous, and properly from the remote joints. And it itself cleanses the stomach and expels from it the superfluities adhering to its villi (Mesué). It purges phlegm and cold chymes and all viscous humors. (Constantinus Afric. 366).

laudabilius est: The best is the white, visibly and finely ground, having pores like those of a thin reed, flat, quickly breakable and not coarse (Avicenna). Mesué, Ibn Massouih, and Hobeïch agree with Avicenna. The yellow and the black Turbith were not used.

asuthi: Asuth was the name used by the Egyptians for a plant that the Greeks called arnoglossus and the Romans plantago (Apulejus Herb. 1.).

vetus cognoscitur: The holes mentioned must not be confused with the fine pores described above. There was much doubt about how the large holes arose. Aboul-Abbas en Nebatz (cited by Ibn el Beïthar) believed they were caused by transport over the sea, since the drug carried overland arrived in good condition. Liber experienc. (cited by Ibn el Beïthar) states that the holes were caused by worms and larvae, and that the worm-eaten drug was harmful and had no laxative effect.

rectificatione: Since Turbith acted weakly and slowly and often caused nausea, it was rectified. Mesué describes three different methods for this.

rade corticem: The procedure is described by Avicenna and is the first one cited by Mesué.

83

antidotis: It was given with Ginger or Mastix.
ne forte adhereat: compare the note on frangatur p. 63. Hobeïch has worded it the same.
oleo roseo aut amigdalarum: The Arabs commonly gave Turbith together with almond oil. The method appears to have been introduced by Rhazes and is mentioned by Avicenna and several others.

VIOLA: The plant under discussion here is Viola odorata, L. According to Dioscorides it was also called the purple Ion, Dasypodion, Priapeion, the wild Ion or Kybelion; the Romans called it Sitialis, Muraria or Viola purpurea. Its Arabic name is Benefsig. The flower was attributed a mild laxative effect, the seeds a stronger one.
frigide: It is cold and moist in the first degree, and some say it is warm in the first degree, but there is no doubt about the coldness of its leaves (Avicenna II, II, 715). Massih (according to Ibn el Beïthar) considered it cold in the first degree and moist in the second; Constantinus Africanus calls it frigida in fine primi gradus, humida in initio secundi. The uncertainty about the nature of the drug is clearly visible in Mesuë (f. XXXIIIIr).
purgant coleram rubeam: Arab physicians generally state that violet removed bile humors from the stomach. Solutione educunt choleram et alterant excessus eius (Mesuë). Choleram rubeam de stomacho et intestinis purgat, calorem eorum mitigat (Constantinus Africanus 344).
turbit: Violet was used as a cooling poultice. Taken internally, where it served partly as a laxative and partly as a diuretic, it was considered a mildly acting remedy, most often given together with other substances or in decoctions of plums, tamarinds, myrobalans, or fumitory. It was also frequently used in sugary solutions, syrups, or sugar-water.

NOTANDUM QUOD OMNIS MEDICINA FORTIS: The rule is analogous to what applied to foodstuffs, which were also given in larger quantities in cold regions and in wintertime. Copho (f. CCCXVr) discusses the matter in the section de consideratione loci: Locus etiam consyderandus, in quo debet dari medicina, an sit calidus, ut in estate propter

84

the heat of the sun; or whether it is too cold, as with the cold of winter or of a region. Compare also the section on much and little matter.

medicina laxativa fortis [strong laxative medicine]: Copho evidently has (in De arte medendi, the section on the diversity of ages) the passage to which the text here refers. It reads: To the elderly and to children we do not give dissolving but only loosening medicine, unless the necessity of illness demands it, nor do we give strong medicines but mild ones. For since the bodies of old people are weak and loosened, if we were to give strong and dissolving medicines, they would be further dissolved and weakened. Similarly indeed not to children; because since the moisture of children is abundant and light, if a dissolving and strong medicine were given, their moisture would quickly be consumed . . . Likewise we do not purge children or old people in summer, on account of the dissolution of their humors which comes from heat, lest an excessive loosening follow from the medicine, except indeed if necessity demands it. In the chapter on the diversity of region in purging, Cophon says expressly: Old people we do not purge on account of the coldness of their constitution. He supports this with an Aphorism of Hippocrates, that in summer the upper bowels are to be purged, in winter the lower (Littré IV, 503), to which Galen attaches the remark: What holds for the seasons of the year holds analogously for regions with respect to heat and cold; and so too it must be understood with respect to ages.

in vere [in spring]: Hipp. Aph. VI, 47 (Littré IV, p. 575).

corpora [bodies]: Hipp. Aph. II, 9 and VII, 71 (Littré IV, p. 473 and 603).

Item non des [Also, do not give]: For in the mixing of purging medicines a conflict arises, since when one of them draws off bile, if it happens, another evacuates phlegm, for both can be evacuated at the same time, but since one acts as quickly as possible while the other by nature is accustomed to move the purging long after administration (Galen: On the Regimen in Acute Diseases, II, cap. 11, Kühn XV, p. 537).

hora debita [the proper hour]: Each humor held sway for six hours: For blood dominates from the ninth hour of the night until the third hour of the day. Bile from the third hour of the day until the ninth hour of the day. Melancholy indeed dominates from the ninth hour of the day until the third hour of the night. Phlegm from the third hour of the night until the ninth hour of the night. But if it is summer, and you wish to purge bile by vomiting, you should give the emetic a little before the hour of day, so that it may linger in the stomach

85

One should work during the hours of choler and purge choler. During these same hours you should give medicine if you wish to purge melancholy downward. If therefore you wish to purge melancholy, you should give medicine before the ninth hour, so that the medicine works during the hours of melancholy and draws it out. But if you wish to purge phlegm, let the patient sleep for three or four hours of the night, and then let the medicine be given before midnight, and he should not sleep afterward. If you wish to purge blood, reduce it in the morning, unless the patient is elderly, or illness, or something else stands in the way. Indeed if you purge a humor during other hours, it sometimes does more harm than good, since the humor that is then dominant is expelled rather than the one that needs to be purged. (Copho: On the art of healing, chapter on the consideration of day and night in purging).

lanam succidam: . . . and unwashed wool, which they call oesyperon, i.e. succidam (Galen's Methodi medendi, book XIV, Kühn X, 965). On the medical use as a soothing agent (mostly for contusions, swellings, etc.) see De simpl. med. temp. ac facult. lib. XI, Kühn XII, p. 348 and Galen's commentary on Hippocrates: De fracturis, Kühn XVIII, p. 524.

times: Here again he carefully derived the indications for remedies from the bodily condition, and at the same time considered the patient's strength — not as something that sometimes indicates the use of remedies, but rather as something that contraindicates and sometimes prohibits them. For it is not the case that because a sick person is strong in body he therefore needs a clyster; rather, the indication for a clyster is derived from the condition of the bowels. If the patient's strength is robust, evacuation is permitted; if it is feeble, it is prohibited. But turn your mind again to Hippocrates' custom, who in such matters sometimes speaks only of strength, yet in the passage cited above also adds age as a consideration. For the chief concern is indeed the patient's strength, but knowledge of age also contributes to assessing it — quickly in children who are sick because their strength flows away readily, while in those in the prime of life it is abundantly sufficient. Moreover, just as in children the body's substance, being both soft and moist, is the chief cause of the dissolution of strength, so too does the situation hold with regard to the seasons of the year. For the heat of these seasons rapidly and simultaneously dissolves the capacity for evacuation (Hippocrates' On the diet in acute diseases and Galen's commentary I, XLIV, Kühn XV, p. 509).

86

scotomiam: see the Practica of Bartholomaeus (Coll. Salernit. IV, p. 374).
mastice: see here Galen: On the simple medicaments, their temperaments and faculties. VIII, Kühn XII, p. 113. [On resins] . . . For beyond the fact that it possesses a mild astringency, such that it is suitable for weaknesses of the stomach, belly, and liver, and for inflammations, it further has in addition a drying quality free from harshness. For it is only minimally sharp and consists of very fine particles. Among others, turpentine is preferred to it, since it clearly possesses a similar though not equal astringency to mastic, but has in addition a certain bitterness, by which it aids digestion even more than mastic does.

pontica: Ponticus is also an "epithet of a certain saline flavor, and denotes salt combined with dregs" (Castelli). Galen does not mention pontica directly.

duos dies: The Practica of Bartholomaeus gives the same time period (l. c. p. 331).

aperi venam: But if the medicine is one of those that are permitted, and it has not acted as a loosening agent, but has caused constriction and gnawing in the belly, and has produced a burning sensation in the body and a dizzy pain in the head together with scotomia, and darkness before the eyes and yawning, we shall hasten to help him with eye-drops and clysters drawing it downward, after the administration of compressive agents that settle it, such as quinces and mastic and similar things. For most such medicines, when driven to the lower part, are overcome by their virtue. But if such remedies do not help and the bad symptoms multiply, and the matter, being made smooth, tends upward, phlebotomy will then be necessary, and specifically from the basilic vein, and after that from the saphena. For this is effective in such a case. (Mesue, Canones univ. Fol. XXIIv).

malicia medicine: Of medicines that loosen the belly, there are some whose harmfulness is great, such that . . . And because these things are harmful, if they have been drunk and bad symptoms arise from them, it will be better for the medicine to be expelled from the body as completely as possible, by vomiting, or by evacuation, and the patient is treated with theriac . . . . . . Also every substance that breaks sharpness by means of a binding, softening, and unctuous quality in which there is adhesiveness is useful for this purpose (Avicenna I, IIII, cap. 9).

non dormiat: nor should he sleep at all while the medicine is working,

87

unless the will is present to restrain it. (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 5 p. 74v).
According to Bartholomeus (p. 332) one should take care that the patient did not
fall asleep; if he did, one should pull him by the hair and
call out to him. What was feared was suffocation: For more often it brings on
suffocation: for the humors retained and stirred up in the stomach
generate a great deal of fumosity, by which fumosity the stomach, filled with
spirits, is compressed, and so suffocation occurs most often in sleep
when the pores are constricted and heat is retained within.

Do not offer food: If the patient's stomach cannot tolerate it,
he should not eat, because his stomach is choleric and quickly
overflows with bile, or because he has strongly abstained from eating
and has endured hunger — let him be given a little bread soaked
in a small amount of wine before the bowel is loosened. (Avicenna
I, IV, cap. 5 p. 74v).

Regarding the solution: He who wishes to drink the medicine and is of a warm
complexion, of weak constitution, and of weak stomach, it will be
better for him to drink it after he has first drunk something, such as
barley water or pomegranate juice, or, to speak universally, after
the stomach has received something subtle and light as nourishment; but he who is not such,
it will be better for him to drink it fasting. (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 5 p. 74v).

A caution to observe: The food of one whose bowel is to be loosened,
or whose vomiting is to be provoked, must be divided: so that what sufficed
him in one day, he eats in many portions, and let the foods be varied, and
the drinks also varied. For from this arrangement it happens to the stomach
that it desires to expel what is in it, either upward or downward. But
from food that is not varied, and when no other food enters the stomach,
the stomach becomes greedy and holds it in with strong retention, especially if
the quantity is small. (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 4).

What is to be feared: After the medicine has ceased working — the sign of which is
that no pain or twisting is felt in the stomach or in the belly —
let broth of chicken or of fish, or of almonds, be given according to what the
time requires. This is given so that the stomach and intestines may be cleansed; if
any of the medicine remains in them, afterward let the patient fast for an hour; then
let a piece of chicken prepared with cumin be given, or let fish be given, or
almond broth; and if the time requires it, let much diluted wine be given,
but let him neither drink nor eat greedily, lest an ephemeral fever follow.

88

On the second day he should go to the bath, taking care to protect himself from cold and exertion for three days, and he should eat foods that generate good humors. (Copho f. CCCXV) Compare also the section on fever caused by a given potion, and Practica Bartholomei p. 333.

excoriation: For one who fears excoriation of the intestines, a bolus of armentus with pomegranate juice should be given, and it is necessary that such things, or similar ones as we have mentioned, be administered after loosening of the bowels (Avicenna, I, IV, cap. 5 p. 75).

who drinks: He also who drinks the medicine is to enter the bath on the second day. And if anything from his humors remains, the bath itself will be able to cleanse it. For if you see that the bath is pleasant to him and he takes delight in it, this will be a sign that the bath itself purifies what has been left behind. Therefore leave him in it; but if you find that he takes no delight in it, and instead suffers heat in it, expel him. (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 5 p. 75).

barley water: Hippocrates: On Diseases, ed. Littré. T. VI, p. 251 § 41.

He should not drink: see the note timendum est, p. 87.

the liver: After loosening of the bowels and frequent phlebotomy, pain often comes on in the liver, which a drink of warm water removes (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 5 p. 75).

in winter: And he who in winter finds it necessary to drink the medicine should watch for a southerly wind. And in summer some of them said the opposite. (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 5 p. 75). Practica Bartholomei says nothing about the winds, but has: "The medicine should be given at the end of spring or the beginning of summer, so that the heat of the day may be avoided." And: "In wintertime in the morning, or during the day, lest the cold of the night impede the effect of the medicine; in autumn the timing is to be determined as in spring; at these times the medicine is to be given, but at other times by no means unless necessity compels." Bartholomeus Anglicus (bk. VII, c. LXIX) has: One medicine is required in winter, another in summer, another at the onset of a disease, another at its height, and another at its decline.

caveat: On the Moon's influence upon human diseases, see Bartholomeus Anglicus (VIII, c. XXIX). The Moon governed the lower part of the abdomen, the intestines and the navel; the Fishes governed

89

The feet too were a sign of rejuvenation (a broad chest, a small head, a flourishing beard and fair complexion make the man of great spirit and round eyes. (VIII, c. XXI). Scorpio ruled the genitals, the kidneys, and the bladder.

Thirst: In those who have taken an evacuating medicine and are not thirsty, the evacuation continues until thirst sets in (Hipp. Aph. IV, 19. ed. Littré IV p. 509, compare also 3. p. 508). Henricus de Dacias text here again leans on Avicenna (I, IV, cap. 6 p. 75v): Among the signs by which one knows the hour at which a purgative should be stopped is thirst. For if the loosening of the bowels persists and thirst does not occur, one need not fear that superfluity has passed through. Yet thirst sometimes occurs even not because of the great quantity of the bowel's evacuation, nor because of its superfluity, but rather because of a disposition of the stomach: for if it be hot, or dry, or both, or in such conditions as these, it is not long before such causes produce thirst quickly, or because of a disposition of the medicine itself, when it is hot and biting, or because of the nature of the matter in itself, since when it is hot, like cholera, or in such conditions as these causes, it will not be long before thirst comes swiftly.

Item, if you are concerned: In Copho (f. CCCXVv) the patient in this case is taken to the bath or placed beside a large fire; he is rubbed on the loins and over the abdomen with warm ointments, and a warm brick is placed on his stomach, "so that the natural warmth may be strengthened and the power of the medicine consumed." Johannes de St. Amando (f. CCLXXv) traces this treatment back to Avicenna.

Si autem: The passage in Galen to which the author alludes is De simpl. med. temp. ac fac., III, cap. 28, (Kühn XI p. 617) but there is no doubt that the text also rests on Avicenna (I, IV, cap. 7, p. 75v): The bowels flow excessively either because of weakness of the veins, or because of the wideness of their openings, or because the medicine irritates those openings, or because some malice of the complexion has been acquired by the body, or because of the course it runs. When therefore the purging of the bowels is excessive, bind the extremities above and below, beginning from the armpits and descending to the groins, binding both, and give in drink a small amount of Theriac or of Philonium, and

90

If you can, make him sweat in a bath, or with the steam of warm water, with his own blankets over him, his head outside; and when he has sweated much, give him the constrictive preparation to drink, and rub him.

Philonum: called majus in contrast to persicum; it was used against cough, pneumonia, spitting of blood, and a great many abdominal complaints (vomiting, liver and spleen diseases, kidney and bladder complaints). Its composition is given in the Antidotarium Nicolai.

constrictiva: of those listed here, Avicenna mentions only one myrtle preparation (Aqua myrtorum).

cicominum: read ciminum; though perhaps cucumer should be read, which finds frequent use in the Practica Bartholomei.

diacodicen: Diacodion, from διά = with and χωδία or χώδνον, the fruit of the poppy.

seruetur a frigido vento: On the influence of winds, see Hippocrates: On Regimen, II, 38 (Littré 6, 531).

si zincopizat: Against syncope, if it supervenes when the patient has not been well purged, rouse the person fainting by the hair or by the beard and nostrils, and sprinkle water over the face; the following remedy also resolves it. (Practica Barth. p. 332).

MEDICINA VOMICA . . . . in attractione humorum: This entire passage has points of contact with, or is a reworking of, Avicenna (I. IV, p. 74. D.): You should know that the attraction of humors which occurs through drinking medicines that loosen the bowels or cause vomiting happens only by the same paths by which they were expelled, until they reach the intestines, and there nature acts to drive them outward. It rarely happens that the humors themselves, when a loosening medicine for the bowels is drunk, ascend to the stomach; and if they do ascend, they will tend toward vomiting. They do not themselves ascend to the stomach for two reasons. The first is that a medicine that loosens the bowels penetrates rapidly to the intestines. The second is that when a loosening medicine for the bowels is drunk, nature hastens to expel the humors themselves from the mesenteric veins downward and not upward, since this is nearer and easier, and because what lies beyond them also compresses them. And this indeed comes from the fact that it moves nature to expel by the nearest paths. But if the medicine has an attractive virtue,

91

which would retain the humors, then the expulsive power of nature would be more worthy, so that in a healthy and strong person it would prevail, even though the medicine does not attract, unless it is along a designated path or toward a marked end. But the arrangement of a medicine that produces vomiting is different from this, because when it is in the stomach it will remain there, and it will draw the humor from the intestines to itself and by its own power overcomes the natural resistance. And you should know that most of the attraction of humors, which medicines draw, indeed comes from the veins, unless it be from a place of great proximity, whereby the attraction will occur from it in the veins and in those things which are not veins, such as humors which are in the lung, which are drawn toward the stomach and intestines on account of proximity, even though they do not travel through the veins. And you should know that most of those things which are desiccating or drying from dry medicines are the cause of evacuating moisture from the body, as happens in dropsy.

Gross humors: Know also that a purgative medicine of the bowels expels that which it evacuates by means of its attractive power, which draws this same humor and perhaps draws the thick and leaves behind the subtle. (Avicenna I, IV, C 6, p. 74.)

Elleborus albus: Helleborus is recommended as an emetic by Hippocrates. (cf. e.g.: On Regimen in Acute Diseases, NOTHA, 25. ed. Littré p. 510).

Condisum is used here as a collective term. Several of the previously mentioned drugs were given preserved.

Nux vomica: If vomiting is administered, then a loosening of the bowels will be more correct. And if it is resistant and cannot be eradicated, then one must make it vomit with those things which are stronger, such as a decoction of nux vomica and mustard and pepper. A medicine causing the phlegm to vomit — let the pith of safflower be dissolved with water of crushed dill and let laurel oil be poured over it (Avicenna III, XIII, T. I, p. 291v).

Sapluie agreste: read salvia agrestis. Wild sage is used by Copho against bloody vomiting.

Ypocras: Aphorisms IV 14, 15. (Littré IV p. 507).

Vomitus Constantini: Constantinus Africanus mentions in his book on natural and non-natural affections of the stomach (p. 241) many different emetics, without it being possible to see which one is an-

92

given by him himself. Among his contemporaries and among subsequent authors, no remedy with the stated name is mentioned.

vomitus patriarche [Patriarch's Vomit]: The composition was: thapsia 1 pound, African saffron 4 drams, cinnamon, asarum each 2 drams, catapuce 2 drams, honey as needed: to be given warm before the onset [of fever] (Antidotarium Nicolai f. CCLIIIv).

vomitus Nicolai [Nicholas's Vomit]: Our vomit remedy is so called from vomiting, because it purges both cold and warm humors; "ours" because it has been composed by us. Take: thapsia (Thapsie) of Palermo or Aragon, collected in the month of May or July, 3 drams; African saffron, 1 dram and a half; nux vomica, half a dram; asarum, 1 dram; asarum honey as needed. The preparation is as follows: in 2 pounds of skimmed honey add 4 drams of asarum juice and boil down to the consumption of the juice; and if you do not wish to use the juice, put in thapsia, asarum each 2 drams and a half, and half of catapuce, and put the whole into sea water and boil until reduced by half, then put into 2 pounds of skimmed honey and cook until the water is consumed; combine with such honey; give in the morning in a quantity the size of a chestnut, with warm water or oxizaccara; for robust persons with the full substance, for the weak the strained liquid only (Antidotarium Nicolai f. CCLIIIr).

Before vomiting . . . . . oxizacari: from oxi, which is called acetum [vinegar] (Joh. de St. Amando fol. CCLVIII).

oxymel: consisted of honey and strong vinegar, in which fennel root and raphanus root were boiled. (Joh. de St. Amando, loc. cit.).

eruca: The things which are preparatory to vomiting are: rocket and radish and [altarich] and fresh [mountain calamint] and onions and leeks and barley water with its sediment, and honey and bean porridge with sweetener and sweet wine and almonds with honey (Avicenna I, IV, p. 76v).

in hora [at the time]: At the time of vomiting, moreover, the eyes should be bound with two compresses (Avicenna I, IV, p. 76v).

post vomitum [after vomiting]: After vomiting is complete, the mouth and face should be washed with vinegar and warm water . . . this is good for two reasons. First, so that the bad matter and the taste of the evil vapor remaining in the mouth may be removed, and therefore the mouth ought to be washed with the face . . . Second, because vomiting harms the teeth (Joh. de St. Amando CCIXXIv).

93

Rufus uses cold water for the face (ed. Daremberg-Ruelle p. 485).

Confortancia: Because vomiting greatly harms the stomach, we must after vomiting strengthen the stomach with astringents and aromatics. (Joh. de St. Amandos, 6th Rule, CCIXXIv).

Excessive vomiting: Excessive vomiting harms the stomach, harms the liver, the lungs, the eye, and sometimes ruptures certain veins (Avicenna I, IV, cap. 14, p. 77).

Against it, first: For the tension and pain that arise under the hypochondria, cloths soaked in hot water and placed on top, along with softening oils, are helpful (Avicenna, loc. cit., cap. 15).

Second: Drinking fatty broths, which are quickly digested, removes the sharp biting sensation remaining in the stomach (Avicenna, loc. cit.).

Third: If hiccup occurs together with it and persists, sneezing will hold it back. (Avicenna, loc. cit.).

Fourth: For the interruption of the voice that occurs after it, it helps to bind the extremities and constrict them, and to place upon the stomach a cloth soaked in oil in which rue has been cooked, and wild cucumber, and to give the patient honey to drink with warm water [fifth]. And for one who has (alsubet), let this be done and let it be put into his ear as well. (Avicenna, loc. cit.).

Make sure: Make sure he sleeps (Avicenna, loc. cit., cap. 16).

Sixth: If the vomiting overflows and humors keep flowing out until blood comes forth, give him four cups of milk mixed with wine to drink: because it suppresses the malice of emetic medicine, prevents bleeding, and soothes the constitution. If you wish to purify the chest and stomach from blood with this remedy, lest anything clot, give him vinegar syrup to drink, whether it be made from honey or from sugar (Avicenna, loc. cit., cap. 16).

Since we have heard ... odor, flavor: The properties of drugs were used in determining the Complexion (see Pract. Bartholomei p. 323-324).

It should be understood: Medicines were divided into maturativa, mollificativa, indurativa, opilativa, rarificativa, and inspissativa, a system that was not strictly maintained but was expanded with many other categories (see Pract. Bartholomei, p. 326).

94

Frons radix: Dioscorides (ed. Sprengel p. 5) says: We, from the very beginning, so to speak, must take care over the years that these things are collected with great discernment, whether in dry or rainy weather: just as it matters that the locations be mountainous, exposed to winds, cold and arid: for the medicinal powers of such plants are stronger.

pluvioso: The Liber servitoris (CCXCII) writes about Seeds, that they should be gathered "before the water falls upon them, by which they would be destroyed."

Montane: And herbs that are gathered in mountainous and harsh lands are of stronger virtue than those which are gathered in valleys and in fat soil and in gardens and orchards (Liber servitoris CCXCVII and Saladin CCCIIv).

Medicaments which are ... of perfection: But it should not be ignored that they very often grow more quickly or more slowly according to the character of the place and the season of the year (Dioscorides p. 6).

flowers: I say that in spring, that is in the months of April and May, herbs should be gathered first and flowers second (Saladin CCCIIv).

seeds: Seeds truly are to be gathered in summer, that is in the month of June or July, because they are then complete (Saladin l. c.).

Roots: Roots truly are to be gathered in autumn, because then the leaves and seeds have fallen, or are dried out, and then the whole virtue of the plants is stored in the roots. (Saladin l. c.) The Liber servitoris says: the time for gathering roots and branches and barks is when their leaves begin to fall. Concerning these conditions Dioscorides says (p. 8): Shrubby plants, while they bear seed, are to be gathered; flowers, however, before they fall of their own accord. But it is proper to strip ripe fruits and seeds while they have begun to dry, before they fall off.

tempus: In Saladin one finds a list of what should be gathered in each month (CCCIIv—CCCIIIr).

humido superfluo: see the note on "pluvioso."

tempus collacionis: herbs should be gathered in calm, clear, non-windy weather (Lib. serv.).

When you have thus gathered ... ligna: Flowers and those things that are fragrant, once gathered, should be stored in linden-wood boxes kept free of moisture. (Dioscorides p. 8).

95

Amber, musk: And it is necessary [= should be stored] that all aromatic substances used for scenting be kept in gold or gilded silver vessels, or in vessels of porcelain, or in glass. (Saladin, patit. VI). Dioscorides uses silver containers for liquid things.

Moist substances: And the storage of moist things, such as juices and liquid gums, confections and electuaries, liquids and similar preparations, should be in thick glass vessels or glazed earthenware or silver or horn, and similar materials (Saladin and Liber serv. CCXCVII). Furthermore, for liquid medicines any denser material is suitable, such as silver, glass, or horn (Dioscorides p. 8–9).

Eye salves: Bronze vessels will be suitable for eye medicines and liquids (Dioscorides, loc. cit.). Saladin says: soft medicines that are appropriate for treating the eyes should be stored in bronze vessels.

Fats: Fats and marrows should be stored in tin vessels (Dioscorides, Saladin).

Oils: Oils should be stored in glass vessels [Saladin].
